metaTitle: Powerwall or Generator? California Outage Backup Compared
metaDescription: Tesla Powerwall 3 vs a 20 kW standby generator for California outages: runtime, fuel, noise, upkeep, PSPS safety and the PG&E rebates that apply in 2026.
h1: Powerwall or Generator? Home Battery vs. Backup Generator in California
intro:
A home battery like the Tesla Powerwall 3 gives you silent, automatic backup with no fuel, but it holds a fixed amount of energy: 13.5 kWh per unit on Tesla's datasheet. A standby generator keeps running as long as its fuel lasts, but it is loud, needs regular exercise and service, and burns fuel you have to supply. For most California outages measured in hours to a couple of days, especially with solar to recharge it, a battery covers the job. For well pumps, medical loads or outages that run for days without sun, a generator does something a battery alone can't.

The money has shifted too. The federal residential clean energy credit no longer applies to batteries installed after 2025, and most SGIP battery budgets are closed or waitlisted. But PG&E now pays $7,500 toward a permanent battery for first-time owners whose accounts have had five or more Wildfire Safety outages since January 1, 2024, and up to $300 toward a qualifying portable generator in high fire-threat areas.

This page compares the two spec for spec, then walks through what each costs to own, how they behave in a multi-day PSPS event, the noise and permit rules, and when the honest answer is both.

sections.heading: Powerwall 3 vs. a 20 kW standby generator, spec for spec
sections.body:
Put the two machines' own spec sheets side by side and the trade-off is clear.

Tesla's Powerwall 3 datasheet lists 13.5 kWh of energy per unit, continuous on-grid output set at installation between 5.8 and 11.5 kW, up to 15.4 kW of off-grid output at the 11.5 kW setting with an 80 A breaker, and a 185 LRA motor-start rating. Up to four Powerwall 3 units and three Expansion units can be combined, for 94.5 kWh. Tesla's warranty is 10 years.

Generac's spec sheet for its 20 kW Guardian standby generator lists 20,000 watts on propane and 17,000 watts on natural gas. At full load it burns 3.56 gallons of propane or 307 cubic feet of natural gas an hour; at half load, 2.39 gallons or 219 cubic feet. It is rated at 67 dB(A) at 23 feet under normal load and 58 dB(A) during its quiet five-minute exercise, which can be set weekly, every two weeks or monthly. The limited warranty is five years.

The runtime arithmetic follows from those numbers. A Powerwall 3 feeding a steady 1 kW of backed-up load would take about 13.5 hours to empty before any solar recharge. The generator at half load on propane uses about 57 gallons in 24 hours. The battery's limit is stored energy; the generator's limit is fuel.

sections.heading: The runtime math nobody wants to say out loud
sections.body:
A battery is a fixed reservoir. Once it's depleted, it stays depleted until the sun comes up (if you have solar feeding it) or the grid comes back. There is no version of a battery-only system that runs indefinitely through a multi-day outage with no sun — that's simple arithmetic, not a knock on the technology.

A natural-gas-fed standby generator, by contrast, runs as long as gas service to the property holds, which in practice is close to indefinite for the length of most PSPS events. A propane-fed unit is capped by tank size — a larger buried tank buys more days, but it's still a countdown, and exactly how many days depends heavily on your specific generator's load and the manufacturer's own sizing chart, not a number this page will guess at for you.

The practical takeaway: if your outage history is measured in hours to a couple of days and you have or want solar, a battery covers it cleanly and silently. If you're in a rural area with well-pump loads, medical equipment, or an outage history that regularly stretches past a few days, a combustion generator's open-ended runtime is doing something a battery physically cannot do alone.

sections.heading: What each actually costs to buy and run
sections.body:
On the battery side, no manufacturer publishes a California installed price, and the installer and blog estimates that circulate online are not a primary source. The closest primary benchmark is LBNL's Tracking the Sun (2024 Edition): storage added roughly $750 to $1,000 per kWh to the installed price of paired residential systems in 2023, nationally. At that rate a single 13.5 kWh unit adds about $10,000 to $13,500, and whole-home coverage usually means stacking two or three units.

On the generator side, a portable unit with a manual transfer switch or interlock kit is the cheapest entry point, and it won't power a full house — expect to run a fridge, some lighting, and maybe a well pump. A whole-house automatic standby unit costs more to buy and install with an automatic transfer switch, and more again if a new gas line or a buried propane tank has to go in. No primary source publishes California installed prices for either, so get itemized quotes for the unit, the transfer switch, the fuel work and the permit.

sections.heading: PG&E's outage rebates change the math in fire country
sections.body:
If PG&E serves you and your area sees repeated wildfire-safety outages, two PG&E programs tilt the comparison.

The Permanent Battery Storage Rebate pays $7,500 once per household after a qualifying permanent battery is installed and gets Permission to Operate. You must be a first-time battery storage customer with five or more Wildfire Safety outages since January 1, 2024, be on a time-of-use rate, pick a battery from PG&E's Qualified Product List bought on or after January 1, 2025, and enroll it in the Emergency Load Reduction Program through your provider. PG&E listed 200 rebates remaining on September 14, 2026, and applications close December 31, 2026 at the latest.

The Generator and Battery Rebate pays up to $300, plus up to $200 more for CARE and FERA customers, toward a portable generator that is CARB-compliant and on PG&E's qualified product list, or a portable battery between 290 Wh and 1 kWh. It applies in Tier 2 or 3 High Fire-Threat Districts, High Fire Risk Areas, or on EPSS circuits, with the same December 31, 2026 cutoff.

PG&E's Residential Storage Initiative goes further for some households: a battery installed at no charge for customers on EPSS circuits with five or more EPSS outages since January 1, 2024 who are enrolled in CARE, FERA, Medical Baseline or the Self-Identified Vulnerable program. Nothing comparable is offered for whole-house standby generators on these PG&E pages.

sections.heading: Noise, permitting, and where you're actually allowed to run one
sections.body:
A battery makes no combustion noise. A standby generator does: Generac's spec sheet for its 20 kW Guardian lists 67 dB(A) at 23 feet under normal load and 58 dB(A) during its low-speed exercise. It runs that loud for as long as the outage lasts, and briefly for every scheduled self-test.

California doesn't set one statewide noise limit for home generators. Limits come from your city or county ordinance and, if you have one, your HOA's CC&Rs, and they often differ by time of day. A generator that's fine to run at 2 p.m. can break a nighttime limit at 2 a.m., which is exactly when you need it during a long outage. Read your ordinance and CC&Rs before buying.

On permitting, both options typically need an electrical permit for the panel tie-in; a standby generator with a new gas line or propane tank adds a plumbing or mechanical permit. CSLB classifies C-10 as Electrical Contractor and C-46 as Solar Contractor. CSLB adopted a rule in 2024 that adds battery storage to the C-10 scope and limits C-46 contractors to incidental batteries up to 80 kWh, but it says the rule's effective date is stayed by court order. Verify any contractor's license and classification at cslb.ca.gov.

sections.heading: Maintenance: none versus a weekly ritual
sections.body:
A home battery has no engine to maintain: no oil, no spark plugs, no fuel to go stale. Over a ten-year horizon, that's nothing to schedule and nothing to forget. Tesla's warranty does ask that a Powerwall stay online and registered for firmware updates to keep the full ten-year term.

A standby generator is the opposite. It exercises itself automatically, five minutes at a time on Generac's 20 kW Guardian, programmable weekly, every two weeks or monthly, burning a little fuel even when there's no outage. That's how it confirms it will start when you need it. Beyond that, expect scheduled service such as oil, filter and plug changes; ask for a service-contract price with the quote. A portable generator has no automatic test at all, which is why so many owners discover a dead one during the outage it was bought for.

sections.heading: The wildfire and PSPS-specific case
sections.body:
During a Red Flag Warning, a combustion generator is a device you're running outdoors, near dry vegetation, producing exhaust heat, in exactly the conditions utilities cut power to avoid sparking a fire in the first place. Safety agencies including the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission have repeatedly flagged carbon monoxide poisoning from portable generators run in garages or too close to windows as a recurring PSPS-season hazard — never run one indoors or in an attached garage, door open or not.

A battery introduces none of that: no exhaust, no fuel stored on-site, nothing running outdoors that could throw a spark. That's the core of the case for a battery as the default backup layer in a high-PSPS area, with a generator held in reserve rather than run continuously.

For your own address's actual PSPS exposure, don't rely on a statewide average — frequency and duration vary enormously by circuit and fire-risk tier. The CPUC publishes event data and an address-level lookup on its Public Safety Power Shutoff dashboard at cpuc.ca.gov; check your specific circuit's history before sizing a system off a guess.

sections.heading: Which incentives still apply, and which are gone
sections.body:
Not long ago, the pitch for a PSPS-area homeowner was simple: SGIP's Equity Resiliency budget discounted a battery heavily and the federal 25D credit took 30% off the rest. Both are gone as planning assumptions.

The IRS says the Residential Clean Energy Credit is not allowed for expenditures made after December 31, 2025, and treats an expenditure as made when the original installation is completed. SGIP closed its ratepayer-funded budgets, including Equity Resiliency, to new applications at the end of 2025 under CPUC Decision 25-12-003. On September 23, 2026 the program's tracker showed the state-funded AB 209 equity budget on a waitlist for PG&E, SCE, CSE, SoCalGas and LADWP customers, with only the budget for customers of publicly owned utilities in PG&E's and SCE's programs open. A waitlist spot is not committed funding.

What's new is utility money aimed at outage-hit homes, covered in the PG&E section above. In a lease or PPA, the company that owns the battery handles any tax benefit; ask it to show you in writing how that affects your price. And before signing anything long-term, remember that installers do fail: Freedom Forever's Chapter 11 case was converted to Chapter 7 liquidation by an order signed August 7, 2026. Check a contractor's license and standing at cslb.ca.gov first.

sections.heading: The hybrid case: when you actually want both
sections.body:
If your home sees PSPS events several times a season, lasting anywhere from a few hours to a couple of days, and you already have or want solar, a battery covers that pattern cleanly with no noise, no fuel runs, and no CO risk. If your property has well-pump loads, medical equipment that can't tolerate any gap, or an outage history that regularly runs past what a battery alone can carry, a generator's open-ended runtime is doing a job the battery can't.

For a lot of whole-house situations in high-PSPS territory, the defensible answer is both, sized for different jobs rather than as redundant backups for the same one: solar plus battery as the daily driver covering routine multi-day PSPS events silently, and a smaller generator (often a portable unit with a manual or interlock switch, sized for critical circuits only) held in reserve for the outlier event that outlasts the battery with no sun to recharge it. That combination costs more upfront than either system alone, so run it only if your actual outage frequency and home load justify covering both cases — not because a sales rep said you need everything.

whenThisIsWrong: Skip a whole-home battery if your outages are genuinely rare, under once a year and measured in an hour or two, and you don't qualify for PG&E's outage rebate; a multi-unit battery is a hard cost to justify against that little exposure. Skip a battery-only strategy if you have well-pump, medical, or other loads that can't tolerate running out when the sun isn't up; that's a generator's job, not a battery's. Skip a whole-house standby generator if your city or HOA's noise ordinance effectively bars running one for hours at a time, or if you're in a Tier 3/4 fire-risk area where combustion equipment running outdoors during Red Flag conditions creates a real ignition and carbon monoxide concern you're not equipped to manage safely. And if you're served by a publicly owned utility — LADWP, SMUD, MID, Anaheim, Roseville, Lodi, Imperial ID, or Turlock ID — the NEM 3.0 export-rate urgency driving a lot of this decision for PG&E, SCE, and SDG&E customers doesn't apply to you the same way; those utilities set their own terms, so get your specific numbers from them before assuming this page's incentive framing carries over.

faqs.question: Powerwall vs generator: which is better for California outages?
faqs.answer: For outages of hours to a couple of days, especially with solar to recharge it, a Powerwall is usually the better fit: silent, automatic, no fuel, no exhaust. For well pumps, medical equipment or outages that run for days without sun, a generator's fuel-limited runtime covers what a 13.5 kWh battery can't. Many high-PSPS homes end up with a battery for routine outages and a small generator in reserve.

faqs.question: Does PG&E give rebates for batteries or generators?
faqs.answer: Yes, both, with conditions. The Permanent Battery Storage Rebate pays $7,500 to first-time battery owners with five or more Wildfire Safety outages since January 1, 2024. The Generator and Battery Rebate pays up to $300, plus up to $200 for CARE and FERA customers, toward a qualifying portable generator or small portable battery in high fire-threat areas or on EPSS circuits. Both close December 31, 2026 at the latest.

faqs.question: Can I still get a federal tax credit for a home battery in California?
faqs.answer: Not for a battery you own that is installed now. The IRS says the Residential Clean Energy Credit (25D), which covered 30% of a battery's cost, is not allowed for expenditures made after December 31, 2025, and an expenditure counts as made when installation is complete. If you lease a battery or buy its output under a PPA, the owner handles any tax benefit; ask the provider to show in writing how it affects your price.

faqs.question: Is the SGIP battery rebate still available in 2026?
faqs.answer: Only in a narrow slice. SGIP's ratepayer-funded budgets, including Equity Resiliency and Small Residential Storage, closed to new applications at the end of 2025. On September 23, 2026 the state-funded AB 209 income-qualified equity budget showed a waitlist for PG&E, SCE, CSE, SoCalGas and LADWP customers; only the budget for income-qualified customers of publicly owned utilities in PG&E's and SCE's programs was open. Check selfgenca.com/home/program_metrics/ before counting any SGIP money.

faqs.question: How long will a whole-home battery actually last during a multi-day PSPS outage?
faqs.answer: It depends on your load and whether you have solar recharging it during the day — there's no single number that applies to every house. A battery sized for whole-home backup without solar will typically run out well before a multi-day event ends if you're running AC, water heating, and full lighting loads. Pairing the battery with solar extends it significantly, since the panels top the battery back up each sunny day of the outage. Ask any installer for a load calculation specific to your panel and appliances, not a generic runtime claim.

faqs.question: Is a generator or a battery better for wildfire-prone, high-PSPS areas?
faqs.answer: For routine PSPS events, a battery is the safer default: no exhaust, no fuel to store near dry vegetation, nothing to run outdoors during a Red Flag Warning. Combustion generators carry real risks in fire season — carbon monoxide poisoning from a portable unit run in a garage or too close to a window is a recurring hazard flagged repeatedly by safety agencies, and an outdoor unit is one more ignition source near vegetation. The tradeoff is runtime: a battery alone can run out during an extended multi-day-plus outage with no sun, which is where a generator kept in reserve — not run continuously — earns its place.

faqs.question: Do I need a permit for a home battery or a backup generator in California?
faqs.answer: Generally yes for both — a battery tied into your electrical panel and a permanently installed standby generator with an automatic transfer switch both typically require an electrical permit, and a standby generator with a new gas line or propane tank usually needs additional plumbing/mechanical sign-off from your local building department. CSLB's own classification list points to C-10 (Electrical Contractor) for this wiring work; solar-tied storage can also implicate a C-46 (Solar Contractor) license depending on scope. Verify any contractor's license number and classification directly at cslb.ca.gov before signing.

faqs.question: Will a standby generator get me in trouble with my HOA or the city?
faqs.answer: It can. Outdoor noise limits in California are set city by city and by HOA CC&Rs, often with lower limits at night, and there's no single statewide number. Generac's 20 kW Guardian is rated at 67 dB(A) at 23 feet under normal load, so running it for hours during an outage, or even its scheduled self-test, can be noticed. Check your ordinance and CC&Rs before buying.

faqs.question: Can I combine solar, a battery, and a backup generator?
faqs.answer: Yes, and for whole-house needs in a high-PSPS area this is often the most defensible answer rather than picking one. Solar plus battery covers routine PSPS events silently with no fuel management. A smaller backup generator, kept in reserve rather than run continuously, becomes the fallback only for the rare extended multi-day-plus event or when the battery runs low with no sun to recharge it. This costs more upfront than either system alone, so it only makes sense if your outage history and load actually justify covering both the routine case and the outlier.

bottomLine: A Powerwall-style battery buys silent, automatic backup with no fuel, sized in fixed kWh: 13.5 kWh per Powerwall 3. A standby generator buys open-ended runtime at the cost of noise, fuel and upkeep: a 20 kW Generac burns about 2.4 gallons of propane an hour at half load. The federal battery credit is gone and most SGIP budgets are closed or waitlisted, but PG&E customers with five or more Wildfire Safety outages since 2024 can get $7,500 toward a battery through December 31, 2026. If PSPS hits your circuit more than once a season, the answer for many homes is both: a battery for routine outages and a small generator in reserve for the long one.

h1: Does a Battery Actually Pay Back Under NEM 3.0 in California?
intro:
SGIP clarification September 10, 2026: Small Residential Storage, Equity Resiliency and ratepayer-funded Residential Solar and Storage Equity are closed in the current tracker. Some residential AB 209 categories are open or waitlisted; broad closure language below refers to the closed categories, not every SGIP pathway. Check the exact category and administrator at selfgenca.com/home/program_metrics/ before counting any rebate.

LBNL’s Tracking the Sun (2024 Edition) estimates that storage added roughly $750 to $1,000 per kWh to the installed price of paired residential systems in 2023, a national figure; at that rate a 13.5 kWh battery adds about $10,000 to $13,500. Whether it pays for itself under NEM 3.0 depends on your utility, your rate plan and your usage, because the underlying math is not the same statewide.

Here is the mechanism in one line. NEM 3.0 — officially the Net Billing Tariff, which has applied to customers applying for interconnection since April 15, 2023 — credits exports at values the CPUC says are "usually lower than the retail rate" but "can rise above the retail rate on late summer evenings." A battery does not make money by exporting solar. It makes money by letting you use your own solar in the evening instead of exporting it for less and buying grid power back at a higher price.

That spread — export credit versus peak retail — is the whole trade, and how wide it runs depends on whether PG&E, SCE, or SDG&E bills you. This page covers only those three. NEM 3.0 does not apply to LADWP, SMUD, or any of California's other publicly owned utilities, and nothing here should be read as urgency if one of those is on your bill.

sections.heading: The core math: export credit versus peak retail
sections.body:
Every battery-payback question under NEM 3.0 reduces to one comparison: what you're credited to export a kilowatt-hour versus what you'd otherwise pay to buy one back in the same hour. The export side is set hourly from CPUC-approved avoided-cost values, which the CPUC says are usually lower than the retail rate. The buy-back side is whatever your rate plan charges at that hour, highest in the evening peak window.

A battery captures the difference by storing midday solar you'd otherwise export and using it that evening instead of buying grid power. It does not capture value by exporting more. NEM 3.0 vintage also matters: the CPUC says residential PG&E and SCE customers who apply to interconnect before the end of 2027 receive slightly higher-than-normal bill credits for exported energy for nine years, and SDG&E customers are excluded. The CPUC also says the original customer is guaranteed use of the tariff for nine years. None of this changes the fundamental shape of the trade.

sections.heading: PG&E: the E-ELEC rate
sections.body:
The CPUC lists E-ELEC as PG&E's approved rate for Net Billing Tariff customers. PG&E's residential average rate was 33.7 cents per kWh as of June 2026, according to the CPUC Public Advocates Office, but an average hides the hourly prices a battery works against.

Pull the E-ELEC price for each time-of-use period from PG&E's current tariff sheet and the hourly export values from PG&E's published export-credit tables. Compare the evening price with the midday export value. That difference, times the kilowatt-hours your battery actually shifts each day, is the yearly value. A proposal that skips those two inputs has not done the PG&E math.

sections.heading: SCE: check which time-of-use plan you are on
sections.body:
The CPUC lists TOU-D-PRIME as SCE's approved rate for Net Billing Tariff customers. SCE's residential average rate was 34.4 cents per kWh as of June 1, 2026 (CPUC Public Advocates Office). SCE's other time-of-use plans, such as TOU-D-4-9PM and TOU-D-5-8PM, have different peak windows and prices, so check which plan your bill names before you run the numbers, and take the prices from SCE's current rate pages rather than from a proposal's summary.

The early-adopter export adder the CPUC describes applies to residential SCE customers who apply to interconnect before the end of 2027. Ask the installer whether its export values include it.

sections.heading: SDG&E: highest average rate, no export adder
sections.body:
The CPUC lists EV-TOU-5 as SDG&E's approved rate for Net Billing Tariff customers. SDG&E had the highest residential average rate of the three utilities, 45.5 cents per kWh as of June 1, 2026 (CPUC Public Advocates Office), and its customers are excluded from the early-adopter export adder that PG&E and SCE customers receive.

A high retail rate widens the gap a battery can capture, but the evening price on your own plan is what matters, so read it from SDG&E's current rate tables and compare it with the hourly export values SDG&E publishes.

sections.heading: SGIP won't help you pay for it
sections.body:
The state rebate that used to soften battery costs is not available to a typical homeowner now. The program administrators' tracker (selfgenca.com, as of September 22, 2026) shows the Small Residential Storage category closed at Step 7 ($0.15 per Wh) for CSE, SCE, SoCalGas and PG&E customers. The ratepayer-funded Residential Solar and Storage Equity category ($1.10 per Wh) and Equity Resiliency ($1.00 per Wh) also show closed. The AB 209 Residential Solar and Storage Equity category ($1.10 per Wh) shows a waitlist for CSE, SoCalGas and LADWP, and it is limited by income and other eligibility rules.

At $0.15 per Wh, the closed general category would have paid about $2,025 on a 13.5 kWh battery. If an installer's proposal still counts an SGIP rebate for your project, ask it to show you, in writing, which category you qualify for and its current status. A waitlist does not promise a rebate.

sections.heading: The federal credit is gone for owned batteries — a PPA is a different calculation
sections.body:
The federal residential clean energy credit (Section 25D) — which covered both solar panels and owned battery storage — does not apply to expenditures made after December 31, 2025, per the IRS. If you buy and own a battery outright now, there is no federal tax credit offsetting its price.

A third-party-owned system — a lease or PPA where the provider keeps title — is a different calculation. The owner, not you, may be able to claim the commercial Section 48E credit, and whether any of that value reaches your payment is a contract question, so ask for it in writing. The tradeoff is counterparty risk — Freedom Forever converted to Chapter 7 liquidation in mid-2026 after filing Chapter 11 that spring, Sunnova filed Chapter 11 in mid-2025 and is now administered by a legacy-portfolio servicer rather than writing new contracts, and SunPower filed Chapter 11 in 2024. If you sign a 20-year PPA, the company on the other end of it needs to still exist in year 15.

sections.heading: How to run the payback math yourself
sections.body:
No primary source publishes a payback period for a NEM 3.0 battery, and this page does not invent one. The arithmetic is simple enough to run on your own numbers.

First, kilowatt-hours shifted per day: the midday solar your battery stores that you would otherwise export, capped by the battery's usable capacity and by your evening use. Second, value per kilowatt-hour shifted: your plan's price in the hours you would otherwise buy from the grid, minus the export credit you give up for that kilowatt-hour. Third, yearly value: kilowatt-hours shifted per day, times value per kilowatt-hour, times 365. Fourth, simple payback: the installed price, less any rebate you have in writing, divided by the yearly value.

For scale, LBNL's 2023 storage premium of $750 to $1,000 per kWh puts a 13.5 kWh battery at roughly $10,000 to $13,500 on top of the solar price. Ask each installer to show those four lines with your own twelve months of usage. A proposal that shows only a payback year is incomplete.

sections.heading: What actually moves your number
sections.body:
Four things swing these numbers more than the utility does. First, how much excess solar your system produces relative to your household load — a battery can only shift power you're actually generating and not using, so an undersized solar array starves the arbitrage. Second, whether you charge the battery from solar only or also from off-peak grid power, which changes which spread applies. Third, financing cost — interest on a battery loan eats into or erases the yearly value; a cash purchase or a very low-rate loan preserves it. Fourth, EV charging: if you're charging a vehicle at home, that load competes with the battery for the same stored solar, and the math has to account for which use gets priority.

None of these four are the same for any two households, which is exactly why a generic 'batteries pay back in X years' claim from an installer should be treated as a sales pitch to verify against your own bill, not a fact to accept.

whenThisIsWrong: A battery arbitrage case falls apart under several common conditions. If you're still grandfathered on NEM 2.0, none of this applies — you likely have a far better export deal already, and adding a battery is a different calculation entirely; don't let anyone push you off that agreement. If your solar system is sized close to your household load with little consistent midday excess, there's not enough surplus power to shift, and the battery mostly just backstops outages rather than earning arbitrage. If you're on LADWP, SMUD, or another publicly owned utility, NEM 3.0 doesn't govern your bill at all — this entire spread analysis is irrelevant to you. If you plan to move soon, a battery may not return your money before you sell; run the four payback steps above first. If financing costs on the battery are high, they can erase the yearly value entirely — run the loan math before the arbitrage math. And if your actual reason for wanting a battery is outage backup rather than bill savings, that's a legitimate but separate decision — don't let a resilience purchase get sold to you as a fast financial payback when the numbers don't support it.

faqs.question: What is the actual NEM 3.0 export credit right now?
faqs.answer: It changes by hour and by month. The CPUC says export credits under the Net Billing Tariff are usually lower than the retail rate but can rise above it on late summer evenings. Residential PG&E and SCE customers who apply to interconnect before the end of 2027 receive slightly higher-than-normal export credits for nine years; SDG&E customers do not. Ask your installer to show the hourly export values it used, and check them against your utility's published export-credit tables before you sign.

faqs.question: Does a home battery pay for itself in California now that SGIP is closed?
faqs.answer: The general-market Small Residential Storage category — which paid $0.15 per Wh at Step 7, about $2,025 on a 13.5 kWh battery — shows closed for CSE, SCE, SoCalGas and PG&E customers on the program administrators' tracker (selfgenca.com, as of September 22, 2026). The AB 209 equity category shows a waitlist for CSE, SoCalGas and LADWP and is limited by income and other eligibility rules. Without a rebate, payback runs on the retail-versus-export spread alone, which is why your utility and rate plan matter more than they used to.

faqs.question: Should I get a PPA/leased battery instead of buying one outright?
faqs.answer: An owned residential battery gets no federal credit: Section 25D does not apply to expenditures made after December 31, 2025, per the IRS. With a third-party-owned system — the provider keeps title, you pay for the power or the lease — the owner may be able to claim the commercial Section 48E credit, and whether any of that value reaches your payment is set by the contract. The tradeoff: you take on counterparty risk with the provider, which matters given how many major national solar companies have gone through bankruptcy in the past two years.

faqs.question: Which utility has the best case for adding a battery?
faqs.answer: There is no single answer. SDG&E had the highest residential average rate of the three in June 2026 — 45.5 cents per kWh, against 34.4 cents at SCE and 33.7 cents at PG&E, per the CPUC Public Advocates Office — which tends to widen the gap a battery can capture, but SDG&E customers do not get the early-adopter export adder that PG&E and SCE customers do. The evening price on your own rate plan, and how much midday solar you would otherwise export, decide the case for your home.

faqs.question: I'm still on NEM 2.0 — does any of this apply to me?
faqs.answer: No. NEM 3.0 (the Net Billing Tariff) only governs systems that interconnected after April 15, 2023. If you're grandfathered on NEM 2.0, you're likely still getting a retail-rate-equivalent export credit, which is a materially better deal than anything described on this page, and adding a battery changes that calculation entirely — get a system-specific review before you touch your existing interconnection agreement.

faqs.question: Does this analysis apply to LADWP, SMUD, or other city-owned utility customers?
faqs.answer: No, and this is worth saying plainly: publicly owned utilities including LADWP, SMUD, MID, Anaheim, Roseville, Lodi, Imperial ID, and Turlock ID are not subject to CPUC jurisdiction and do not follow NEM 3.0 at all. They set their own net metering and export terms. None of the urgency or spread math on this page should be applied to a POU bill — that utility's own tariff is the only document that matters.

faqs.question: What about backup power during outages — does that change the payback math?
faqs.answer: Yes, but it's a separate decision from the pure dollars-and-cents arbitrage covered here. If you're weighing a battery partly or mainly for outage resilience, the value of keeping the lights, fridge, and medical equipment running during a PSPS event or grid failure doesn't show up in a cents-per-kWh spreadsheet. That's a legitimate reason to buy a battery even where the arbitrage payback alone is marginal — just be clear with yourself and any installer about which reason is actually driving the purchase, because the sales pitch tends to blend the two.

bottomLine: A battery in California is not a blanket yes or a blanket no under NEM 3.0 — it's a utility- and plan-specific spread calculation. The CPUC says export credits are usually below the retail rate, so a battery earns its keep by replacing evening grid purchases with your own stored solar. SGIP's general-market category is closed, and the federal 25D credit for an owned battery does not apply to expenditures after December 31, 2025. A third-party-owned system may carry a Section 48E credit for its owner, which trades a subsidy question for counterparty risk. Get your actual rate plan, your actual usage and the hourly export values before signing anything, and treat any contractor's payback claim as a starting point to verify, not a fact to accept.

h1: What a Home Battery Actually Costs in California in 2026
intro:
SGIP clarification September 10, 2026: Small Residential Storage, Equity Resiliency and ratepayer-funded Residential Solar and Storage Equity are closed in the current tracker. Some residential AB 209 categories are open or waitlisted; broad closure language below refers to the closed categories, not every SGIP pathway. Check the exact category and administrator at selfgenca.com/home/program_metrics/ before counting any rebate.

LBNL’s Tracking the Sun (2024 Edition) estimates that storage added roughly $750 to $1,000 per kWh to the installed price of paired residential systems in 2023, a national figure; at that rate a 10 kWh battery adds about $7,500 to $10,000. For a typical homeowner there is now no federal tax credit and no state rebate cushioning that number. Section 25D does not apply to expenditures made after December 31, 2025. The Self-Generation Incentive Program's general-market category is closed for every administrator that runs it. Two of the biggest levers homeowners assume are still there are both gone or exhausted right now.

That doesn't mean a battery is a bad idea. Under NEM 3.0, California's net billing regime, the CPUC says the credit for exported solar is usually lower than the retail rate you pay to import power, which is exactly the gap a battery is built to close. But the honest payback math depends on your specific utility, your specific rate schedule, and a hardware price that varies more by brand and installer than most quotes let on.

This page walks through what a battery costs per usable kWh, what installation and panel work add on top, why SGIP and the federal credit won't help you right now, and where the industry's own numbers are shakier than they look. Where we couldn't verify a figure independently, we say so — that's the point of this page existing.

sections.heading: The Two Incentives You Thought You Had Are Both Gone
sections.body:
Start here, because this changes the entire calculation and most homeowners shopping for a battery right now don't know it yet.

The federal Residential Clean Energy Credit, Section 25D, covered battery storage of at least 3 kWh capacity alongside solar equipment. The IRS says the credit does not apply to expenditures made after December 31, 2025, and an expenditure is made when the installation is completed. If you install a battery you own outright in 2026, there is no federal credit attached to it. Full stop.

SGIP, California's Self-Generation Incentive Program, is the other lever homeowners expect. The program administrators' program-metrics page, as of September 22, 2026, shows the Small Residential Storage tier — the one a typical, non-income-qualified homeowner would apply under — sitting at Step 7 and closed across every utility territory it covers: PG&E, SCE, SDG&E/CSE, and SoCalGas. That's not a reduced rate. It's exhausted.

There are narrower equity tiers: Residential Solar and Storage Equity for income-qualified households in disadvantaged communities ($1.10/Wh, Step 6, also closed), Equity Resiliency for medical-baseline, high-fire-district, or PSPS-impacted customers ($1.00/Wh, also closed per the same data), and a San Joaquin Valley variant ($1.10/Wh, also closed). The AB 209 equity category ($1.10/Wh) shows a waitlist for CSE, SoCalGas and LADWP, so if you think you qualify, check your administrator's status rather than assuming either way; a waitlist does not promise a rebate. For the ordinary homeowner reading this page, the practical fact is: SGIP money is not available right now.

sections.heading: What a Battery Costs Per Usable kWh
sections.body:
No primary source publishes a California installed price for a home battery. The closest national benchmark is LBNL's Tracking the Sun (2024 Edition), which estimates that storage added roughly $750 to $1,000 per kWh to the installed price of paired residential systems in 2023. At that rate a 10 kWh battery adds about $7,500 to $10,000 and a 13.5 kWh battery about $10,000 to $13,500. Treat it as a benchmark for reading a quote, not a quote itself.

Usable capacity varies by brand, and this is where you should anchor your comparisons rather than sticker price alone. A Tesla Powerwall 3 delivers 13.5 kWh usable, an Enphase IQ Battery 5P 5 kWh and a FranklinWH aPower 2 15 kWh, per each manufacturer's datasheet. Ask any installer quoting a specific brand to break out hardware, labor and any adders separately, and compare cost per usable kWh across at least two brands before signing.

sections.heading: Installation, Panel Upgrades, and Permitting: The Costs Nobody Leads With
sections.body:
The battery itself is rarely the whole bill. Three categories of add-on cost show up on almost every real installation, and they're the ones sales quotes tend to gloss over.

Installation labor: ask for it as its own line, so you can compare it across quotes.

Electrical panel upgrades come up often when a battery and existing solar system push a home's electrical service past what an older 100-amp panel can handle safely. No primary source publishes a California price for that upgrade, so ask your installer directly whether your existing panel needs work, and get the upgrade priced as its own line, before you get a final number.

Permitting costs and timelines are the least standardized part of this whole process. They vary by city and county — the Authority Having Jurisdiction, or AHJ — and we found no reliable statewide source for typical permitting fees or turnaround times. Some California jurisdictions have adopted expedited solar-and-storage permitting; many haven't. Ask your installer to name the permit fee and expected timeline for your specific city or county before you sign a contract, not after.

sections.heading: Brand by Brand: What You're Actually Buying, and Where the Old Numbers Lie
sections.body:
Usable capacity is the cleanest apples-to-apples comparison available, because current installed pricing by brand is not something a primary source publishes.

Tesla Powerwall 3: 13.5 kWh usable capacity, per Tesla's datasheet. Older installed-price figures circulating online often describe the Powerwall 2, which Tesla has been phasing out, not the Powerwall 3. Don't use them to budget a 2026 quote.

Enphase IQ Battery 5P: 5 kWh usable capacity, per Enphase's datasheet. Older price figures for Enphase batteries may be hardware-only rather than fully installed, so check what a quoted figure includes.

FranklinWH aPower 2: 15 kWh usable capacity, per FranklinWH's datasheet.

Generac PWRcell, LG Energy Solution RESU Prime, SolArk, and Panasonic EverVolt: if an installer quotes you one of these brands, ask for the usable capacity in kWh and the total installed price, then do the division yourself — don't accept a sticker price without that math.

sections.heading: The NEM 3.0 Payback Math, Honestly
sections.body:
Here's the mechanism a battery is supposed to exploit: under NEM 3.0 (California's net billing tariff for PG&E, SCE, and SDG&E customers), the CPUC says the credit you get for exporting excess solar is usually lower than the retail rate, though it can rise above it on late summer evenings. Meanwhile, the CPUC Public Advocates Office put the June 2026 residential average rate at 33.7 cents per kWh at PG&E, 34.4 cents at SCE and 45.5 cents at SDG&E, and evening time-of-use prices run above those averages.

That gap is the entire case for a battery under net billing. Instead of exporting your midday solar surplus for a low credit, you store it and use it yourself in the evening, avoiding the higher import price.

No primary source publishes a payback period for a battery under NEM 3.0, and this page does not invent one. The number depends on your export values, your time-of-use schedule, how much solar you would otherwise export and the installed price. Ask your installer for a payback estimate built from your actual 12 months of utility bills and your utility's current published rate schedule, not a generic industry number.

sections.heading: Third-Party Ownership and the 48E Wildcard
sections.body:
A battery installed under a third-party-owned arrangement — a lease or a power purchase agreement, where a company rather than the homeowner owns the equipment — is outside Section 25D, which applies to property the taxpayer owns. The owner may be able to claim the commercial Section 48E credit instead.

Whether any of that value reaches you is a contract question. If a PPA or lease provider tells you their battery qualifies for a tax benefit that reduces your cost, ask them to name the specific IRS code section and show in writing how it changes your payment, rather than taking a sales rep's word.

sections.heading: Who's Actually Installing These Batteries Right Now
sections.body:
Before you sign with anyone, know who's still standing. Three of the biggest national names in residential solar and storage have gone through bankruptcy in the past two years, and one of them stopped operating entirely.

Freedom Forever filed Chapter 11 in April 2026 and later moved to Chapter 7 liquidation. It is no longer operating, and homeowners with contracts, warranties or financing tied to it were affected.

Sunnova filed Chapter 11 in June 2025. The company was sold, and its legacy customer portfolio is now administered by SunStrong — which is servicing existing contracts, not originating new ones.

SunPower filed Chapter 11 in August 2024.

None of this means every installer is unstable, and it doesn't mean a battery is a bad purchase. It means the installer's financial stability is now a legitimate line item in your due diligence, the same way you'd check a contractor's license and insurance. Ask directly: who holds the equipment warranty, who's on the hook for service calls in year five, and what happens to your contract if the company you're signing with today doesn't exist in three years.

sections.heading: Publicly Owned Utilities: This Urgency Doesn't Apply to You
sections.body:
Everything above about NEM 3.0 export rates and the arbitrage case for a battery applies to customers of California's investor-owned utilities — PG&E, SCE, and SDG&E — because those are the utilities the CPUC's net billing tariff actually governs.

If you're a customer of a publicly owned utility — LADWP, SMUD, MID, Anaheim, Roseville, Lodi, Imperial Irrigation District, or Turlock Irrigation District — CPUC's NEM 3.0 rules do not apply to you. These utilities set their own net metering and export compensation terms independently. They also set their own retail rates, which are not in the CPUC Public Advocates Office report; compare your utility's own rate schedule with the 33.7 to 45.5 cent June 2026 averages at the big three investor-owned utilities.

Both of those facts push in the same direction: less urgency, and a smaller arbitrage gap for a battery to close. If you're on one of these municipal utilities, don't let a sales pitch built on NEM 3.0 fear apply pressure that doesn't actually describe your situation. Ask your own utility for its current net metering and export terms before you evaluate whether a battery pencils out for you specifically.

If you're on a publicly owned utility like LADWP, SMUD, MID, or one of the irrigation districts, NEM 3.0 doesn't apply to you and your import rate is already lower — the arbitrage case is much weaker or absent. If your monthly usage and bill are already low, a battery may never pay back inside the equipment's warranty life. If you don't already have solar, a standalone battery without generation to charge it from makes far less sense — you'd be paying grid rates to charge it. If you're planning to sell or move within a few years, you likely won't hold the asset long enough to recoup the cost. If your only goal is outage backup and you already own or could buy a portable or standby generator for a fraction of the price, compare the generator's price with the battery's before choosing. And if you'd need to finance the entire cost on a high-interest personal loan rather than cash or a low-rate product, the interest can erase the savings a battery is supposed to generate.

faqs.question: Is there any federal tax credit left for a home battery in California in 2026?
faqs.answer: Not if you buy and own the system outright. The IRS says the Residential Clean Energy Credit (Section 25D) does not apply to expenditures made after December 31, 2025. Battery storage of at least 3 kWh was an eligible expense under that credit while it existed. If you bought and installed a battery in 2026, that federal offset is gone. Third-party-owned systems (a lease or PPA where a company owns the equipment) may still route through a different, commercial-side credit — see the section on that above — but that path does not apply to a battery you purchase and own yourself.

faqs.question: Can I still get an SGIP rebate for a home battery?
faqs.answer: For a typical, non-income-qualified homeowner, no — not right now. The program administrators' tracker, as of September 22, 2026, shows the Small Residential Storage general-market category ($0.15/Wh, Step 7) closed for CSE, SCE, SoCalGas and PG&E. The ratepayer-funded Residential Solar and Storage Equity category ($1.10/Wh) and Equity Resiliency ($1.00/Wh) also show closed. The AB 209 equity category shows a waitlist for CSE, SoCalGas and LADWP, so if you think you qualify, check your administrator's status rather than assuming either way; a waitlist does not promise a rebate.

faqs.question: What does a 10 kWh battery actually cost installed, all-in?
faqs.answer: No primary source publishes a California installed price. LBNL's Tracking the Sun (2024 Edition) estimates that storage added roughly $750 to $1,000 per kWh to the price of paired residential systems in 2023, nationally, which works out to about $7,500 to $10,000 for 10 kWh. Treat it as a benchmark, not a quote. Get two or three itemized quotes from licensed installers — brand, inverter type, and whether your panel needs upgrading all move the number.

faqs.question: Which battery brand is the best value per kWh?
faqs.answer: No primary source publishes brand-by-brand installed prices, so this page does not rank them. Usable capacities from manufacturer datasheets: Tesla Powerwall 3 at 13.5 kWh, Enphase IQ Battery 5P at 5 kWh, and FranklinWH aPower 2 at 15 kWh. Older installed-price figures circulating online often describe the Powerwall 2, not the Powerwall 3 — don't use them to budget. Divide each quote's installed price by its usable kWh to compare.

faqs.question: Does a battery actually pay for itself under NEM 3.0?
faqs.answer: It can, but no primary source publishes a payback period, and this page does not invent one. The CPUC says export credits under NEM 3.0 are usually lower than the retail rate; the CPUC Public Advocates Office put June 2026 residential averages at 33.7 cents per kWh (PG&E), 34.4 cents (SCE) and 45.5 cents (SDG&E). That gap is what makes storing your own solar output more valuable than exporting it. The exact export values depend on your utility's current tables and your time-of-use schedule, so pull them directly from your utility before you accept a payback number an installer gives you verbally.

faqs.question: Does any of this apply if I'm on LADWP, SMUD, or another municipal utility?
faqs.answer: Largely no. Publicly owned utilities — LADWP, SMUD, MID, Anaheim, Roseville, Lodi, Imperial Irrigation District, Turlock Irrigation District — are not subject to CPUC-mandated NEM 3.0 net billing. They set their own net metering, export terms and retail rates. That changes the arbitrage math a battery is supposed to solve. If you're a customer of one of these utilities, ask them directly for their current net metering terms rather than assuming NEM 3.0 urgency applies to you.

faqs.question: Is it true a major installer went out of business?
faqs.answer: Yes. Freedom Forever filed Chapter 11 in April 2026 and later moved to Chapter 7 liquidation — it is no longer operating, and homeowners with existing contracts were affected. Sunnova filed Chapter 11 in June 2025; it was sold, and its legacy portfolio is now administered by SunStrong, which is not originating new contracts. SunPower filed Chapter 11 in August 2024. If any installer quoting you a battery is affiliated with these names, or resembles their financing structure, ask directly who holds the warranty and who services the equipment if the installer stops operating.

bottomLine: No primary source publishes a California installed price for a home battery; LBNL's national 2023 benchmark of roughly $750 to $1,000 per kWh of storage is the closest reference, and there aren't any incentives worth counting on for a typical owned system. Section 25D does not apply to expenditures after December 31, 2025, and SGIP's general-market category is closed. That leaves the math resting on two things: what you pay to import power (June 2026 residential averages of 33.7 to 45.5 cents per kWh at PG&E, SCE and SDG&E) and the export credit you give up, which the CPUC says is usually lower. If you're on a municipal utility like LADWP or SMUD, NEM 3.0 doesn't touch you and the case looks different. Get a written, itemized quote — hardware, labor, panel work, permits — before you sign anything, and check that your installer will still be in business next year.

metaTitle: How Many Home Batteries Do You Need?

h1: How Many Batteries Do You Actually Need in California?
intro:
Most California homes that get quoted a two-battery system only need one. That is the blunt version, and it matters more this year than last. The federal residential Clean Energy Credit (25D) stopped covering any property placed in service after December 31, 2025 — battery storage included — per the IRS, whose credits-and-deductions page (last updated July 4, 2026) states the cutoff in plain language. The state rebate that used to backstop battery costs, SGIP, has also gone dark for new applicants: as of September 5, 2026, the program's own step tracker at selfgenca.com lists the general-market storage step and the wildfire/medical-baseline equity resiliency step both as closed to new reservations in every investor-owned utility territory. Closed does not mean zero dollars left on the books — the same tracker still shows residual, unspent funds in each step — but it does mean the step is no longer accepting new applications, so a homeowner signing a contract today cannot count on that money.

That means every kilowatt-hour of battery capacity you buy this year gets no 30 percent tax credit and no open rebate step behind it. You are paying full retail for whatever size a contractor writes on the proposal, so getting the size right is worth real money, not just peace of mind.

Sizing a home battery is not a guess. It is arithmetic: how many kWh you draw in the evening peak, how many circuits need to survive an outage, and which utility you are on. This page walks through that math and tells you plainly when a second unit earns its cost — and when it is an upsell you do not need.

sections.heading: Start With Your Bill, Not the Installer's Battery Chart
sections.body:
Before anyone quotes you a battery, pull twelve months of utility bills and find two numbers: your usage during the peak time-of-use window (typically 4-9pm for PG&E, SCE, and SDG&E) and your total daily average. Those two numbers, not a state-average figure, are what should size your system, because California household usage varies enormously by climate zone, home size, and whether you have a pool pump or a heat pump. A coastal condo and an inland Sacramento Valley house with a swamp cooler are not the same customer, and a single statewide average will mislead you either way. If your utility does not show peak-window usage on the bill itself, most utility apps break down hourly usage — pull that data before you sign anything.

Once you have your peak-window kWh, you are doing real math instead of trusting a slide deck. If your evening peak runs 8-12 kWh, a single battery in that range covers it. If a proposal jumps straight to 27 or 40 kWh without asking for your bill first, that is the tell that you are being sized to the product line, not to your house.

sections.heading: Three Different Jobs a Battery Can Do
sections.body:
"How many batteries" is really three separate questions wearing one label. Load-shifting (TOU arbitrage) means charging off cheap or solar power during the day and discharging through the expensive evening peak — no outage protection, pure bill management. Partial backup means a defined set of critical circuits (refrigerator, Wi-Fi and router, some lighting, a well pump, medical equipment) stay powered through an outage, routed through a dedicated critical loads panel. Whole-home backup means everything in the house, including central air conditioning and an electric range, keeps running — which is a dramatically bigger load than the other two.

The gap between the tiers is large. A refrigerator, router and a few lights draw far less energy over a day than central air conditioning, an electric range and a well pump, so whole-home backup can take several times the stored energy of an essential-circuits panel. Your own bill and your installer's load calculation give the numbers for your house.

sections.heading: What a Single Battery Actually Covers
sections.body:
For load-shifting only, that same study puts a single 6-10 kWh battery as typically sufficient — no partial or whole-home backup involved. For partial backup on essential circuits, a single battery around 10 kWh can carry roughly three days of essential-load draw in most locations per the cited study.

In hardware terms, current single units in this range include a Tesla Powerwall 3 (13.5 kWh nominal AC battery energy, up to 11.5 kW continuous output per published specs), an Enphase IQ Battery 5P (5.0 kWh usable capacity and 3.84 kVA continuous output per unit, commonly stacked two or more), and a FranklinWH aPower 2 (15 kWh AC usable capacity and 10 kW continuous output, per the manufacturer's current datasheet). Manufacturers revise capacity, output, and pricing tiers periodically — pull the current datasheet from your contractor before you sign, do not quote spec-sheet numbers from an old brochure or a Claude answer as gospel.

sections.heading: Do the Arithmetic: Turning Your Bill Into a Battery Count
sections.body:
The sections above tell you to pull your peak-TOU and daily-average kWh off your bill. Two worked checks turn that into an actual battery count: one for usable kWh (does a day's energy fit), and one for continuous kW (can the battery push out what your chosen circuits draw at once).

Usable-kWh check (example numbers only — use your own bill): say your peak-TOU window runs about 9 kWh on a typical day. One Enphase IQ Battery 5P (5.0 kWh usable, per Enphase's datasheet) covers close to half of that; two units (10.0 kWh) clear it with margin for a weaker solar day. One Tesla Powerwall 3 or FranklinWH aPower 2 (13.5-15 kWh usable, per their datasheets) clears the same window in a single unit.

Continuous-kW check (example numbers only — use your installer's load calc): say the circuits you'd actually put on backup — refrigerator, some lighting and outlets, Wi-Fi/router, garage door, and a well pump when it cycles — add up to roughly 2.5 kW of running draw, with the pump's start-up surge briefly higher. A single Enphase 5P (3.84 kVA continuous) or FranklinWH aPower 2 (10 kW continuous) clears that on paper; so does a Powerwall 3 configured at 5.8 kW or above (Tesla's four continuous-power tiers run 5.8, 7.6, 10, and 11.5 kW). The number that actually decides whether you need a second unit is more often continuous kW under a motor's starting surge than total kWh — ask your installer for the surge/LRA rating against your largest single motor, not just the running total.

sections.heading: How Many Can You Stack, Per Manufacturer
sections.body:
Raw capacity isn't unlimited — each system has a published ceiling, set by the battery's own hardware or by its gateway or controller. A Tesla Powerwall 3 holds 13.5 kWh of nominal AC battery energy per unit and can be configured for 5.8, 7.6, 10, or 11.5 kW of continuous output; natively, Tesla supports up to 4 Powerwall 3 units plus 3 Expansion units (7 total, roughly 94.5 kWh), while an AC-coupled install through Backup Gateway 2 supports up to 10 Powerwalls. An Enphase IQ Battery 5P holds 5.0 kWh of usable energy per unit at 3.84 kVA continuous output (7.68 kVA peak in backup); its IQ System Controller 3 supports up to 40 kWh of 5P capacity without a separate power control system (8 units) or 80 kWh with one (16 units). A FranklinWH aPower 2 holds 15 kWh AC per unit at 10 kW continuous discharge (8 kW charge, 15 kW peak for 10 seconds), and FranklinWH's required aGate controller supports up to 15 units per aGate — up to 225 kWh total.

Two figures elsewhere on this page have been updated to match: the hardware-examples paragraph above and the FAQ comparing the three brands both used to cite an older FranklinWH aPower figure (roughly 13.6 kWh, roughly 5 kW continuous). FranklinWH's current shipping unit, the aPower 2, is rated at 15 kWh AC and 10 kW continuous, per the manufacturer's own datasheet — the number used throughout this page now.

sections.heading: What the Gateway or Controller Changes About Your Number
sections.body:
Battery kWh isn't the only ceiling. Each system routes backup power through a separate piece of hardware, and that piece has its own limits. Tesla's Backup Gateway 2 sits between your meter and panel and decides what's on the backed-up side; in a native, non-Gateway-2 install, one Powerwall 3 acts as the system controller for the others. Enphase's backup mode requires the IQ System Controller 3, whose Neutral-Forming Transformer is rated at 3,600 VA continuous — a separate number from total battery capacity, and one your installer should size against your backed-up circuits, not just against 5P count. FranklinWH's aGate is the required controller for every aPower 2 install; it's what sets the 15-unit stacking limit above.

In every case, how much of your home you can actually run at once is also capped by your electrical panel or a dedicated critical-loads subpanel — whole-home backup, not just battery count, is often a panel conversation with your installer. For a full spec-by-spec comparison of all three systems — efficiency, backup-mode detail, and app or monitoring features — see our Powerwall vs. Enphase vs. FranklinWH comparison.

sections.heading: The Critical Loads Panel Nobody Explains Upfront
sections.body:
A critical loads panel (or an automatic transfer switch built into the battery's own gateway hardware, which is how Tesla, Enphase, and Franklin systems increasingly handle it) is what separates "the battery is installed" from "the battery actually keeps your fridge and Wi-Fi running in a blackout." Without it, a whole-home-wired battery either backs up everything (needing the bigger, whole-home-sized battery from the section above) or backs up nothing selectively — there is no in-between unless the critical circuits are physically separated onto their own panel.

This add-on has real installed cost on top of the battery itself, and it varies by how many circuits get separated and whether it is a manual or automatic setup. Get a specific line-item number from your contractor's written quote rather than accepting a round figure — this is exactly the kind of cost that gets glossed over verbally and then shows up as a surprise on the invoice.

sections.heading: Why the Incentive Collapse Changes the Sizing Conversation
sections.body:
Two years ago, a homeowner who bought a slightly oversized battery had a 30 percent federal credit and, in many cases, an SGIP rebate softening the mistake. Neither exists now in the same form. The 25D credit does not apply to expenditures after December 31, 2025. SGIP's general-market storage category and its Equity Resiliency category — historically the safety-net bucket for wildfire and medical-baseline customers — both show closed on the program's tracker as of September 22, 2026.

That combination removes most of the financial cushion that used to make "buy a little extra capacity, just in case" a low-stakes decision. With no federal credit and no open rebate step to apply to, nearly every additional kWh above what your bill math actually supports is now a dollar-for-dollar cost with no offset. If a proposal recommends two batteries, ask the installer to show you, using your own peak-window usage, why one is not enough — not why two is safer.

sections.heading: When Two Batteries Actually Make Sense
sections.body:
A second unit is a real decision for a specific set of homes, not a default upgrade. That includes all-electric households running a heat pump for both space and water heating alongside Level 2 EV charging, where evening and overnight draw genuinely exceeds single-unit capacity. It includes homes with a well pump, since well pumps draw a large surge current that eats into continuous-output headroom fast. It includes households that want true whole-home HVAC backup through a multi-day outage — which can take two or three units at current single-unit capacities. And it includes homes in high-PSPS-risk wildfire zones where multi-day outages are a recurring reality rather than a once-a-decade event.

What it does not automatically include: a standard single-family home on a normal TOU rate with no EV, no well pump, and no all-electric heating. That profile is a one-battery household in the large majority of cases, and if you were told otherwise without anyone asking for your bill, get a second opinion before you sign.

sections.heading: Your Utility Changes the Math
sections.body:
If you are served by PG&E, SCE, or SDG&E, you are on the CPUC's Net Billing Tariff (NEM 3.0), where the CPUC says export credits are usually lower than the retail rate and vary by hour and season. The CPUC Public Advocates Office put residential average rates at 33.7 cents per kWh at PG&E, 34.4 cents at SCE and 45.5 cents at SDG&E as of June 2026. All three move with each utility's rate cases, so treat these as a snapshot, not a fixed number. That gap is the reason batteries matter now: exporting excess solar for a low credit and then buying power back at the evening price makes storing it yourself the better trade, once the math works for your usage pattern. Check your own utility's current published export-credit table and rate schedule before assuming a number.

If you are served by a municipally owned utility instead — LADWP, SMUD, MID, or similar publicly owned utilities like Anaheim, Roseville, Lodi, Imperial Irrigation District, or Turlock Irrigation District — none of the NEM 3.0 discussion above applies to you. Publicly owned utilities are not subject to CPUC jurisdiction and set their own net metering and rate terms. SMUD and MID both price power on tiered and time-of-day schedules rather than one flat rate, so pull the current residential rate schedule from each utility's own site (ladwp.com, smud.org, mid.org) rather than relying on a statewide average. The NEM 3.0 urgency driving battery sales in IOU territory does not exist on a muni bill in the same way; get your own utility's actual export and rate terms before accepting a sizing pitch built around NEM 3.0.

sections.heading: Hardware and Contractor Risk Before You Sign
sections.body:
The battery you buy is only as good as the company standing behind the warranty. Freedom Forever filed Chapter 11 in Delaware on April 15, 2026. After creditors rejected a proposed sale of the company to its own CEO, Freedom Forever told the bankruptcy court on July 31, 2026 that it intended to convert to liquidation; the judge signed the order converting the case to Chapter 7 effective August 7, 2026, and appointed a trustee. It is no longer operating as a going concern. Sunnova filed Chapter 11 in June 2025; its assets sold, and its legacy portfolio is now administered by SunStrong rather than the company that originally signed the contract. SunPower filed Chapter 11 in August 2024. None of this means every battery from these companies stopped working — it means the entity contractually obligated to honor a workmanship or performance warranty may no longer exist in the form that signed your paperwork.

Before signing with any installer, ask directly whether they are still an operating going concern, whether the battery manufacturer's warranty is backed by the manufacturer itself (Tesla, Enphase, and Franklin all warrant their own hardware independent of the installer) rather than a since-liquidated installer's in-house warranty, and who services the equipment if the installer folds. On licensing: California requires a CSLB-licensed contractor, and industry practice treats battery storage installation as falling under either a C-10 Electrical or C-46 Solar contractor's license — there is no separate battery-specific classification. Confirm the specific license number and classification directly with CSLB (cslb.ca.gov, 1-800-321-2752) before signing, rather than taking a salesperson's word for it.

whenThisIsWrong: Skip a second battery, and possibly skip a battery entirely, in these cases. If you are a renter or plan to move within a few years, the payback math on any battery size rarely closes before you leave. If you are on a publicly owned utility (LADWP, SMUD, MID, Anaheim, Roseville, Lodi, Imperial ID, Turlock ID) with a favorable net metering arrangement, the NEM 3.0 export-credit collapse driving battery urgency elsewhere in California does not apply to your bill, and you should get your own utility's numbers before assuming you need storage at all. If outages in your area are rare (no PSPS exposure, not in a high fire-threat zone) and you are not chasing TOU arbitrage, a battery may just be an expensive appliance. If your household is small, well-insulated, and on a lower TOU spread (some municipal and some standard residential rates), a single small unit or no battery may beat a two-unit system on payback period. And if your proposed budget cannot also cover a properly sized critical loads panel or transfer switch, buying the battery without it means you are paying for backup capacity you cannot actually direct to the circuits that need it.

faqs.question: Do I need a battery at all if I already have solar panels?
faqs.answer: Not automatically. Under NEM 3.0, the CPUC says PG&E, SCE, and SDG&E customers' export credits are usually lower than the retail rate, so a battery that lets you use your own solar in the evening peak instead of exporting it can add value. But if you are on a publicly owned utility with different net metering terms, or your usage pattern does not create a large evening peak, solar without storage can still make financial sense on its own. Run your own bill numbers before assuming storage is mandatory.

faqs.question: Is there any rebate left for home batteries in California as of September 2026?
faqs.answer: As of September 22, 2026, the Self-Generation Incentive Program's tracker at selfgenca.com shows the general-market Small Residential Storage category and the Equity Resiliency category (the wildfire and medical-baseline safety net) both closed for PG&E, SCE, SoCalGas and CSE customers. The AB 209 equity category shows a waitlist for CSE, SoCalGas and LADWP. Check the tracker yourself before assuming either way, and do not plan your battery budget around a rebate that is not confirmed open on the day you sign.

faqs.question: Does the battery still qualify for a federal tax credit if I add it to existing solar?
faqs.answer: No. The IRS states plainly that the residential Clean Energy Credit (25D), which covered battery storage with at least 3 kWh of capacity at a 30 percent rate, is not available for any property placed in service after December 31, 2025. That applies whether the battery is standalone or paired with solar you already own. A battery purchased and installed in 2026 gets no federal credit under this program, full stop.

faqs.question: How much backup time does one battery actually give me?
faqs.answer: It depends on what is on the backed-up side. Runtime is the battery's usable kWh divided by the average kW your backed-up circuits draw. Essential circuits such as a refrigerator, Wi-Fi and some lighting draw little, so one battery can carry them for a long time; whole-home backup with air conditioning running eats through the same capacity far faster, which is why whole-home coverage needs several times the capacity of partial backup, not just a little more.

faqs.question: Is a Tesla Powerwall, Enphase battery, or FranklinWH unit better for a California home?
faqs.answer: Each covers a different capacity and output profile per unit: current published specs put the Powerwall 3 around 13.5 kWh usable with roughly 11.5 kW continuous output, an Enphase IQ 5P around 5 kWh and 3.84 kW per unit designed to be stacked, and a FranklinWH aPower 2 around 15 kWh and 10 kW continuous. Which fits depends on your peak-load surge needs (Powerwall 3's higher per-unit output matters more if you're backing up AC or a well pump) versus wanting granular capacity added in smaller increments (Enphase's stackable model). Pull current datasheets before deciding, since manufacturers revise these figures.

faqs.question: What happened to Freedom Forever, and does it affect my existing battery?
faqs.answer: Freedom Forever filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in Delaware on April 15, 2026. After a proposed sale of the company to its own CEO fell through, the case converted to Chapter 7 liquidation effective August 7, 2026 (the company told the court of its intent to convert on July 31), meaning it is no longer operating and is winding down rather than reorganizing. The battery hardware itself, if made by a third party like Tesla or Enphase, typically carries its own manufacturer warranty independent of the installer — check your specific warranty documents to see whose name is actually on the guarantee.

faqs.question: What license should my battery installer have?
faqs.answer: California requires a CSLB-licensed contractor, and industry practice treats battery storage installation as falling under a C-10 Electrical or a C-46 Solar contractor's license, with no separate standalone classification specifically for batteries. Ask for the contractor's license number and confirm its classification and standing directly through CSLB (cslb.ca.gov or 1-800-321-2752) before signing anything, rather than relying on a verbal claim.

faqs.question: How long will a solar battery last at night, or power my house?
faqs.answer: For your own home, runtime is usable kWh divided by the average kW your backed-up circuits are actually drawing, and that draw shifts constantly as things cycle on and off. Use the usable-kWh and continuous-kW checks above with your own bill and your installer's load calc — a load calculation from your installer, not a spec sheet, gives you the draw side of that math. See our guide on what a battery actually backs up during a Public Safety Power Shutoff for how that plays out in a real outage.

faqs.question: Is there a runtime calculator?
faqs.answer: Not one we publish, for the same reason: a fixed number would imply a guarantee this page can't make. Use the usable-kWh and continuous-kW checks above with your own bill and your installer's load calc instead.

faqs.question: What's the FranklinWH battery's usable capacity?
faqs.answer: The current aPower 2, per FranklinWH's own datasheet, is 15 kWh AC per unit, stacking up to 15 units (225 kWh) per aGate. An older, lower figure for a previous aPower model still circulates in some solar industry material — the aPower 2 is FranklinWH's current shipping unit, and the number this page now uses throughout.

faqs.question: How many solar panels and batteries do I need together?
faqs.answer: This page answers the battery side. For panel count and system-kW sizing, see our guide on how big a solar system you need in California.

bottomLine: Size to your evening peak first, not to a sales rep's chart. Pull your last 12 months of bills, find your 4-9pm usage, and for load-shifting or partial backup you will often land on a single battery — a Tesla Powerwall 3, an Enphase 5P bank, or one FranklinWH aPower, depending on brand. Two units only earn their keep when you are running an all-electric home with a heat pump and EV charging, backing up a well pump, or genuinely need whole-home HVAC coverage through a multi-day outage. As of September 22, 2026, there is no federal credit and no open general-market SGIP category to cushion an oversized system, so every extra kWh is effectively full retail cost with no subsidy behind it. Get your utility's export-credit table before you assume solar will offset the bill, confirm your installer's parent company is actually still operating given the wave of 2025-2026 bankruptcies, and treat "you need two for whole-home backup" as a claim to verify against your own circuit list, not a default to accept.

h1: Tesla Powerwall 3 vs. Enphase IQ Battery 5P vs. FranklinWH aPower 2
intro:
A Tesla Powerwall 3 holds 13.5 kWh and can be field-configured to push out up to 11.5 kW continuous. An Enphase IQ Battery 5P holds 5.0 kWh usable and tops out at 3.84 kVA. A FranklinWH aPower 2 holds 15 kWh and delivers 10 kW continuous, 15 kW for ten-second bursts. Those three numbers alone tell you these aren't interchangeable boxes competing on the same spec — they're three different bets about how a home battery should be built and sold.

Tesla bundles a hybrid solar inverter into the battery itself. Enphase builds the battery out of six small grid-forming microinverters with no single point of failure. FranklinWH builds a big single unit that couples to any existing solar inverter through a separate controller. Each approach has a real, mechanical reason to prefer it for a specific house — and a real reason to avoid it for a different one.

If you are weighing FranklinWH against Powerwall specifically, the short version: the aPower 2 stores more per unit (15 kWh against 13.5 kWh), carries a longer warranty (15 years or 60 MWh against 10 years) and couples to any existing solar inverter through its aGate, while the Powerwall 3 has a solar inverter built in, weighs less and is the simpler choice for a new solar-plus-storage install. The head-to-head section below lays out the spec-sheet numbers. The rest of the page compares all three on capacity, output, coupling, scalability, warranty terms, rebates, and what happens to your battery's warranty when the company that installed it goes bankrupt — which, as of September 2026, is not a hypothetical.
