sections.heading: Three different architectures, not three flavors of the same thing
sections.body:
Tesla Powerwall 3 is fundamentally a DC-coupled all-in-one unit: it has an integrated hybrid inverter with six MPPTs and up to 20 kW of DC solar input built into the same box as the battery. That's the standard configuration for a new solar-plus-storage install. But Powerwall 3 can also run AC-coupled to an existing separate solar inverter through Tesla's Backup Gateway 2, which supports up to 10 AC-coupled Powerwalls — in that mode the Powerwall becomes its own site controller and the Gateway's controller function switches off. It is genuinely both, depending on how the installer configures it, and any comparison that flattens it to just "DC-coupled" or just "AC-coupled" is oversimplifying.

Enphase IQ Battery 5P is 100% AC-coupled by design, with no DC input and no MPPTs on the unit itself. What makes it structurally different from the other two is that it isn't a single battery with one inverter — it's six embedded IQ8D-BAT grid-forming microinverters working in parallel inside one enclosure. There's no single point of failure the way a Powerwall's or aPower's central inverter represents. It also retrofits cleanly onto an existing Enphase microinverter solar array, which the other two can't do without an AC-coupling adapter.

FranklinWH aPower 2 is AC-coupled and inverter-agnostic — it pairs with any existing solar inverter, which makes it the most flexible retrofit option of the three for a house that already has panels from any manufacturer. It requires FranklinWH's aGate controller to function as a full energy-management system across solar, grid, generator, and EV — that's a mandatory add-on, not an option, and it adds real cost.

sections.heading: FranklinWH aPower 2 vs. Tesla Powerwall 3, head to head
sections.body:
Most people who search 'Franklin Powerwall' are choosing between these two, so here they are side by side, using only each manufacturer's own datasheet.

Storage per unit: the aPower 2 lists 15 kWh usable; the Powerwall 3 lists 13.5 kWh. Continuous output: FranklinWH lists 10 kW; Tesla lets the installer set 5.8, 7.6, 10 or 11.5 kW on-grid, and up to 15.4 kW off-grid at the 11.5 kW setting with an 80 A breaker. Short bursts: FranklinWH lists 15 kW for 10 seconds and 25 kW for 1 second; Tesla lists a 185 LRA motor-start rating. Charging: the aPower 2 lists 8 kW of charge power.

Efficiency is stated differently. FranklinWH lists 90 percent round trip, grid to battery to load. Tesla lists 89 percent for solar to battery to home or grid, and 97.5 percent for solar straight to the home or grid through its built-in inverter.

Warranty: FranklinWH lists 15 years or 60 MWh of throughput. Tesla's US limited warranty (revision 2.6, effective May 6, 2026) covers 10 years with 70 percent energy retention at 10 years, unlimited cycles for self-consumption, time-based control and backup, and 37.8 MWh for other uses. Tesla adds that if the Powerwall lacks an internet connection for an extended period or isn't registered, it may not honor the full ten years, but will honor at least four.

Scaling and size: up to 15 aPower 2 units per aGate for 225 kWh on 120/240 V service, against 4 Powerwall 3 units plus 3 Expansion units for 94.5 kWh. The aPower 2 weighs 357 lb; the Powerwall 3 weighs 291.2 lb installed. Both list an operating range of -4°F to 122°F.

The practical split: on a new install, the Powerwall 3's built-in solar inverter (up to 20 kW DC, six MPPTs) saves a component. On a house with existing solar from any brand, the aPower 2 couples through the aGate, while the Powerwall 3 is limited by Tesla to 7.68 kW AC of existing solar per Powerwall on the backup side, or 10 kW with Expansion units.

sections.heading: Capacity, output, and what that means at the breaker panel
sections.body:
Powerwall 3's output is field-selectable at install: 5.8 kW, 7.6 kW, 10 kW, or 11.5 kW continuous AC, with max apparent power to 11,500 VA at the top setting. Off-grid, PV-only discharge can reach 15.4 kW, but only if the on-grid setting is locked to 11.5 kW and the installer runs an 80A breaker with sized conductors — a detail that matters for panel-capacity planning and should be discussed with your installer before assuming you'll get that number. Load-start capability is 185 LRA, enough to start most single AC compressors without a soft-starter.

Enphase's 5P delivers 3.84 kVA continuous at 240V (3.33 kVA at 208V), with a 3-second peak to roughly 7.68 kVA and 48A LRA start capability. Because each unit is only 5.0 kWh, whole-home backup on a typical California house means stacking three or four units — which raises labor and wiring cost per kWh delivered compared to a single larger box, even though the hardware itself scales cleanly.

FranklinWH's aPower 2 delivers 10 kW continuous and 15 kW peak for 10 seconds, with 8 kW continuous charge power — the highest continuous output per single unit of the three. For a house with a well pump, HVAC compressor, and other simultaneous heavy loads during an outage, that per-unit headroom is a real advantage over needing multiple smaller units to hit the same instantaneous draw.

sections.heading: Scalability: how big can each system actually get
sections.body:
Tesla caps a single system at 4 Powerwall 3 units (each with its own inverter) plus up to 3 Expansion units (battery-only, no inverter, floor-mount only, not field-serviceable individually, and compatible only with Powerwall 3 — not with older Powerwall 2 or Powerwall+). That's 7 total units, 94.5 kWh, and per Tesla's own marketing copy, up to 44 kW combined output at the top end.

Enphase's ceiling depends on the controller: up to 4 IQ Battery 5P units (20 kWh) on an IQ System Controller 3G without a power control system, or up to 8 units (40 kWh) on an IQ System Controller 3 with PCS enabled. Some secondary sources claim a 16-unit, 80 kWh ceiling — that contradicts Enphase's own support-page FAQ and shouldn't be relied on; treat 40 kWh as the real ceiling until Enphase publishes otherwise.

FranklinWH scales the furthest on paper: up to 15 aPower 2 units per aGate controller, 225 kWh total — but only on standard 120/240V split-phase residential service. On 208V service (relevant for some California multi-family and ADU-adjacent properties), the datasheet caps it at 2 units per aGate. If your property runs 208V, confirm this with your installer before assuming the 225 kWh figure applies.

sections.heading: Warranty terms: read past the headline year count
sections.body:
Tesla's Powerwall 3 warranty is 10 years, with 70% energy retention guaranteed at 10 years and unlimited cycles for solar self-consumption, time-based control, and backup use, per Tesla's US limited warranty (revision 2.6, effective May 6, 2026). Other uses are capped at 37.8 MWh of aggregate throughput. The same document says Tesla needs an internet connection to deliver firmware updates for the full ten-year term: if the Powerwall is offline for an extended period or isn't registered, Tesla says it may not honor the full ten years, but commits to at least four. Keep the unit online and registered, and confirm registration before your installer leaves. The warranty also transfers to a later owner who can show proof of ownership.

Enphase's IQ Battery 5P carries a 15-year warranty (or 6,000 cycles, whichever comes first) with over 60% capacity retention guaranteed. At roughly one cycle per day, 6,000 cycles works out to about 16.4 years — so the cycle cap and the term roughly align for a typical daily-cycling household, but a heavy user pulling multiple cycles a day could hit the cycle ceiling before the 15-year clock runs out.

FranklinWH's aPower 2 carries a 15-year warranty tied to a 60 MWh aggregate throughput cap, matching Enphase's term length and beating Tesla's 10-year headline number. What FranklinWH does not publish, as of this research, is a stated capacity-retention percentage at the end of that term — Tesla commits to 70% at 10 years, Enphase to over 60% at 15 years, and FranklinWH has not published a comparable number in its datasheet or in any verified secondary source. That's a real gap in what the company discloses, not a knock on the hardware — but don't let anyone tell you FranklinWH matches the other two on this point until they publish a number.

sections.heading: App, monitoring, and the installer-bankruptcy problem nobody puts in the brochure
sections.body:
Enphase's datasheet is the only one of the three that explicitly calls out open API integration alongside its Installer Platform and consumer app — relevant if you want a system that talks to third-party home-energy software. Tesla and FranklinWH each offer only their own proprietary mobile app, with no API integration claim in either datasheet.

Here's the part that matters more than any app screenshot: California has already lost a major installer this year. Freedom Forever filed Chapter 11 on April 15, 2026 in the U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the District of Delaware. After a proposed sale to company insiders fell through, it asked the court on July 31, 2026 to convert the case to Chapter 7 liquidation, and the judge signed that order on August 7, 2026 — the company no longer operates. If Freedom Forever installed your battery, the safe assumption is that you need to check your paperwork regardless. The manufacturer's warranty on the hardware itself — Tesla, Enphase, or FranklinWH, all backed directly by the manufacturer, not the installer — should still hold. What does not survive is any separate workmanship warranty your now-defunct installer wrote on top of it. Ask any installer you're considering, in writing, what happens to your workmanship coverage if they close.

We found no verified, primary-sourced data this research cycle on installer-network size or market share for any of the three brands in California — claims of specific percentages circulating online trace to low-authority SEO content, not manufacturer or industry data, and we're not repeating them here.

sections.heading: Which battery fits which house
sections.body:
A new-build solar-plus-storage install with no existing panels is Powerwall 3's best case — the integrated hybrid inverter removes a design step and reduces installer complexity, and its per-unit output (up to 11.5 kW configurable) covers most whole-home backup needs with one or two units.

A house that already has an Enphase microinverter solar array is the clearest fit for the IQ Battery 5P — it retrofits without an AC-coupling adapter, and the distributed six-microinverter architecture means no single component failure takes the whole battery offline. It's the right call for a smaller, space-constrained install or a homeowner who wants precise control over exactly how much capacity to add, unit by 5.0 kWh unit.

A house with high simultaneous loads during an outage — a well pump plus HVAC compressor plus other heavy draws at once — and an existing non-Enphase solar inverter is the strongest case for FranklinWH's aPower 2, given its 10 kW continuous / 15 kW peak per-unit output and inverter-agnostic AC coupling. Its OSHPD seismic certification (AC 156 / OSHPD / IEEE 693-2005 high, per the aPower 2 datasheet's compliance table — the same standard used for California hospital facilities) is also a notable, if underreported, compliance data point for anyone weighing CA-specific installation standards. The tradeoff: the mandatory aGate controller adds cost, and the unit itself is the largest and heaviest of the three at 357 lb.

sections.heading: Which system fits NEM 3.0 export-shifting vs. whole-home backup
sections.body:
These are two different jobs, and the three systems aren't equally good at both.

Buying mainly to shift solar export under NEM 3.0 — storing daytime solar to use in the evening instead of exporting it for a lower credit — usually means you want to size storage to your actual evening load, not buy more capacity than you'll cycle daily. The Enphase IQ Battery 5P's 5.0 kWh module size is built for that: you add capacity in 5 kWh increments rather than committing to 13.5-15 kWh up front. A single Powerwall 3 or aPower 2 can still do export-shifting, but their per-unit capacity is sized more for backup than for a strictly evening-shifting strategy — excess capacity isn't wasted if you also want outage protection, but it's not the efficient buy if export-shifting is the only goal.

Buying mainly for whole-home backup — keeping HVAC, a well pump, an EV charger, and general household load running together during an outage — favors continuous and peak output over pure capacity. FranklinWH's aPower 2 (10 kW continuous, 15 kW peak) is built for simultaneous heavy loads from a single unit. A Powerwall 3 configured to its top continuous rating (11.5 kW) covers most whole-home scenarios with one or two units. Reaching comparable output from Enphase 5P units requires stacking several 5.0 kWh/3.84 kVA modules plus a System Controller — workable, but it's a different design path than a single higher-output unit.

Most homeowners want some of both. For sizing your own system against your actual bill and load rather than a spec sheet, see our sizing guide, How many batteries do I need in California. For the utility-by-utility export-credit math behind the NEM 3.0 side of this decision, see our battery payback under NEM 3.0 page.

sections.heading: Ecosystem and Installer Lock-In, Stated Neutrally
sections.body:
Each of these three systems ties you to specific companion hardware and, to some degree, to an installer network trained on that brand. None of this is a reason to avoid a system — it's a cost-of-switching question worth asking before you sign.

Tesla Powerwall 3 is designed around Tesla's own hardware: an integrated hybrid inverter in its native configuration, or a Backup Gateway 2 if you're adding it AC-coupled to existing solar. Expanding later generally means more Tesla-compatible hardware, and installation is typically done by Tesla-certified installers. Enphase IQ Battery 5P assumes an Enphase ecosystem — it retrofits cleanest onto an existing Enphase microinverter array, and backup mode specifically requires Enphase's IQ System Controller 3 INT. It's the only one of the three whose datasheet states an open API for third-party monitoring, which is a partial offset on the software side even though the hardware ecosystem is proprietary. FranklinWH aPower 2 requires its aGate controller as mandatory companion hardware, regardless of which solar inverter you already have. That's what makes it inverter-agnostic on the solar side — but it locks the storage system itself into FranklinWH's own controller and app.

What locks you in is the companion hardware, not the installer — ask what a future capacity add-on costs and requires before you commit to one ecosystem.

sections.heading: Does SGIP Eligibility Change by Which System You Pick?
sections.body:
No. California's Self-Generation Incentive Program pays a per-kWh rebate based on installed storage capacity, your utility territory and your household's eligibility — not on battery brand (CPUC). A 13.5 kWh Powerwall 3, a stack of Enphase 5P units totaling 13.5 kWh, and a 15 kWh aPower 2 are evaluated by the same $/Wh mechanics. What decides whether SGIP pays anything is whether your budget has money: the ratepayer-funded budgets closed to new applications at the end of 2025, and on September 23, 2026 the income-qualified AB 209 equity budget showed a waitlist for PG&E and SCE electric customers and for CSE, SoCalGas and LADWP, with only the budget for customers of publicly owned utilities in PG&E's and SCE's programs open. For the live per-utility status, see the SGIP battery rebate status page.

Brand does matter for one California incentive. PG&E's $7,500 Permanent Battery Storage Rebate requires a battery on PG&E's Qualified Product List and enrollment in the Emergency Load Reduction Program through your battery provider. PG&E names Tesla's Virtual Power Plant with PG&E and Enphase's Virtual Power Plant program as enrollment paths; other batteries go through PG&E's Automated Response Technology program. The rebate also requires five or more Wildfire Safety outages on your account since January 1, 2024.

sections.heading: Questions to Ask Any Installer Before You Sign
sections.body: Which specific model and configuration are you quoting, and does the continuous-power number on your quote match the manufacturer's own datasheet for that configuration? Is the install AC-coupled or DC-coupled with your existing solar, and does that change the output or the companion hardware you're paying for? Is the required companion hardware — Backup Gateway 2, IQ System Controller, or aGate — included in the quoted price, or itemized separately? Is the installer a manufacturer-certified installer for this specific brand, and what happens to your workmanship warranty if their company closes? Is SGIP funding actually reserved for your project, or only “eligible” on paper — what changes on your contract if the budget closes before installation? Are you buying mainly for whole-home backup, evening export-shifting under NEM 3.0, or both — and does the system size on your quote match that goal? And what is the unit's manufacturer-stated round-trip efficiency and capacity-retention guarantee, in writing, for the exact model you're buying?

whenThisIsWrong:
Skip all three, at least on a cash or loan purchase, if you're buying storage purely to chase a federal tax credit — Section 25D ended December 31, 2025, with no phase-down, and it applies equally to every brand here. None of these batteries restores that credit.

Skip SGIP as a reason to move fast. On selfgenca.com's tracker checked September 23, 2026, the ratepayer-funded budgets are closed, and the income-qualified AB 209 equity budget is waitlisted everywhere except for customers of publicly owned utilities within PG&E's and SCE's programs. That's a narrow exception, not a reason to rush.

Skip Enphase's 5P if your home needs more than 40 kWh of backup or draws heavy simultaneous loads — you'll need so many units that labor cost per kWh delivered gets worse than a single larger box, and the per-unit continuous output (3.84 kVA) won't start large single loads without stacking units.

Skip FranklinWH if your service is 208V and you were counting on the 225 kWh scaling figure — the datasheet caps 208V installs at 2 units per aGate, a very different ceiling.

Skip any of these if you're on a publicly owned utility (LADWP, SMUD, MID, Anaheim, Roseville, Lodi, Imperial ID, Turlock ID) and were told NEM 3.0 export-rate pressure makes a battery urgent — those utilities set their own net-metering terms and aren't subject to CPUC NEM 3.0, so the urgency argument that applies to PG&E, SCE, and SDG&E customers doesn't automatically apply to you.

faqs.question: FranklinWH or Powerwall 3: which is better?
faqs.answer: Neither wins outright. On the datasheets, the FranklinWH aPower 2 stores more per unit (15 kWh against 13.5 kWh) and carries a longer warranty (15 years or 60 MWh against Tesla's 10 years with 70% retention), and it couples to any existing inverter through its aGate. The Powerwall 3 has a built-in solar inverter, weighs less, and suits a new solar-plus-storage install. Pick by your house: existing solar and heavy simultaneous loads lean FranklinWH; a new system with room for a single wall unit leans Powerwall 3.

faqs.question: Which of these three batteries has the longest warranty?
faqs.answer: Enphase's IQ Battery 5P and FranklinWH's aPower 2 both carry 15-year warranties, longer than Tesla Powerwall 3's 10-year term. But term length isn't the whole story: Enphase guarantees over 60% capacity retention at 15 years, Tesla guarantees 70% at 10 years, and FranklinWH has not published a capacity-retention percentage for its 15-year term in its datasheet or in any verified secondary source as of this writing. A longer term with an unpublished retention guarantee isn't automatically the stronger warranty — ask FranklinWH's installer directly for that number in writing before you compare it head to head with the other two.

faqs.question: Can I get a federal tax credit for any of these batteries in 2026?
faqs.answer: Not on a battery you own that is installed now. The IRS says the Section 25D Residential Clean Energy Credit is not allowed for expenditures made after December 31, 2025, and an expenditure counts as made when the original installation is completed. That applies identically to Tesla, Enphase, and FranklinWH. In a lease or PPA, any tax benefit belongs to the company that owns the equipment, and whether any of it shows up in your rate is set by the contract.

faqs.question: Is SGIP still worth applying for with any of these batteries?
faqs.answer: For most California homeowners, no. The ratepayer-funded SGIP budgets closed to new applications at the end of 2025 under CPUC Decision 25-12-003. On September 23, 2026, selfgenca.com's program-metrics page showed the income-qualified AB 209 equity budget on a waitlist for PG&E and SCE electric customers and for CSE, SoCalGas and LADWP. The one open budget was for income-qualified customers of publicly owned utilities within PG&E's and SCE's programs. If you are not in that group, don't count SGIP in your budget.

faqs.question: What happens to my battery's warranty if my installer goes out of business?
faqs.answer: The manufacturer's warranty on the battery itself — Tesla, Enphase, or FranklinWH — is backed by the manufacturer rather than the installer, so it should remain valid regardless of the installer's solvency. Tesla's warranty also transfers to a later owner with proof of ownership. What doesn't survive is any separate workmanship warranty the installer wrote on top of it. This is directly relevant in 2026: Freedom Forever filed Chapter 11 on April 15, 2026 and was converted to Chapter 7 liquidation by court order on August 7, 2026. If it installed your system, get the warranty registration and workmanship status in writing from whoever services it now.

faqs.question: Which battery is easiest to add onto an existing solar system?
faqs.answer: It depends on what you already have. If your existing array uses Enphase microinverters, the IQ Battery 5P retrofits without an AC-coupling adapter. FranklinWH's aPower 2 AC-couples to existing solar inverters through its aGate, which makes it a flexible retrofit for a mixed or unknown-brand array. Tesla says Powerwall 3 is compatible with all major inverter brands when AC-coupled, but its design guide limits existing solar on the backup side to 7.68 kW AC per Powerwall, or 10 kW with Expansion units.

faqs.question: How much do these batteries actually cost installed in California?
faqs.answer: None of the three manufacturers publishes a consumer installed price, and this page does not repeat installer or blog estimates. The closest primary benchmark is national: LBNL's Tracking the Sun (2024 Edition) estimates that storage added roughly $750 to $1,000 per kWh to the price of paired residential systems in 2023. Get a written, itemized quote for the exact model and configuration, including the Backup Gateway 2, IQ System Controller or aGate, and divide the installed price by the usable kWh to compare brands.

faqs.question: Does the battery brand matter for PG&E's $7,500 rebate?
faqs.answer: Only through two requirements: the battery has to be on PG&E's Qualified Product List, and it has to be enrolled in the Emergency Load Reduction Program through your provider. PG&E names Tesla's and Enphase's virtual power plant programs as enrollment paths, with its Automated Response Technology program for other batteries. The main test is your account: five or more Wildfire Safety outages since January 1, 2024.

bottomLine: Powerwall 3 is the strongest default for a new solar-plus-storage build, with an integrated hybrid inverter and configurable output up to 11.5 kW continuous. Enphase's IQ Battery 5P is the clear pick if you already own Enphase microinverters or want distributed, no-single-point-of-failure architecture in a smaller footprint. FranklinWH's aPower 2 wins on raw per-unit output (10 kW continuous, 15 kW peak) and inverter-agnostic retrofitting, at the cost of a mandatory controller and no published capacity-retention number. None of the three restores the federal tax credit that expired December 31, 2025, and SGIP is closed to nearly every new California applicant — the one live opening is a narrow income-qualified track, not a regional exception. Get every pricing, warranty, and workmanship-coverage claim in writing before you sign — especially given how many installers have gone bankrupt in the past two years.

h1: SGIP in California: battery rebate status, who qualifies and what it pays
intro:
SGIP, the Self-Generation Incentive Program, is the CPUC's rebate for batteries and other equipment installed on the customer's side of the meter. As of September 23, 2026, the general-market home battery budget is closed everywhere. The only residential money left is the income-qualified Residential Solar and Storage Equity budget, which pays $1.10 per watt-hour of storage and $3.10 per watt of new solar.

That budget is open only for customers of publicly owned utilities assigned to PG&E or SCE. For PG&E, SCE, SDG&E, SoCalGas and LADWP customers it is waitlisted. The 2026 SGIP Handbook sets June 30, 2028 as the last day for new and waitlist applications. The official tracker updates nightly, so recheck it before you sign anything.

sections.heading: What SGIP is and who runs it
sections.body:
The CPUC describes SGIP as incentives for distributed energy resources on the customer's side of the meter, including solar paired with storage. The state does not mail you a check. Five program administrators run it: PG&E, SCE, SoCalGas, the Center for Sustainable Energy for SDG&E's territory, and LADWP.

There were two pots of money. Ratepayer-funded budgets came from utility bills. The 2026 SGIP Handbook says administrators issued reservations from those budgets only through December 31, 2025, that December 30, 2025 was the last day to apply, and that every ratepayer-funded waitlist closed that day. The second pot is Assembly Bill 209 money: $280 million from the state's Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund, which CPUC Decision 24-03-071 assigned to the Residential Solar and Storage Equity budget. That is the part still taking applications.

sections.heading: What each residential budget pays
sections.body:
Residential budgets pay per watt-hour of battery capacity. Small Residential Storage, the general-market budget for homes, stepped down to its seventh and final step at $0.15 per Wh. Equity Resiliency paid a flat $1.00 per Wh. San Joaquin Valley Residential and the Residential Solar and Storage Equity budget pay $1.10 per Wh, and the equity budget also pays $3.10 per watt for a new solar system. Only the equity budget still has money for homes.

The handbook's worked example shows the ceiling. A 13.2 kWh battery at $1.10 per Wh comes to $14,520, and 5 kW of solar at $3.10 per W comes to $15,500, for a maximum of $30,020. The actual award can be lower. A project that reports a total eligible cost above 90 percent of that maximum must send receipts for equipment and labor before it is paid, and electrical and critical-loads panel upgrades count toward eligible cost only up to $3,500 per project.

sections.heading: Who qualifies for the equity budget
sections.body:
The handbook's single-family test has two paths. Your household income is at or below 80 percent of the area median income, shown with your most recent federal tax documents. Or your income was already verified because you are enrolled in CARE, FERA, the Energy Savings Assistance program, SASH or DAC-SASH. If you qualify through CARE, FERA or ESA and are dropped from that program before the incentive is paid, the application is cancelled.

Apartment buildings use a different test: five or more deed-restricted low-income units in a disadvantaged community, or a building where at least 80 percent of households earn 60 percent of area median income or less. Those projects must pass at least 51 percent of the solar output to tenants as virtual net metering credits.

Three other rules catch people. AB 209 money is open to any California residential customer, including customers of city utilities and rural cooperatives. The solar incentive covers only a new system, not panels added to an existing array. And a renter needs a letter showing the owner approved the installation.

sections.heading: Which administrator handles your application
sections.body:
If a city utility or electric co-op serves your home, your AB 209 administrator is assigned, not chosen. The official assignment table sends customers of SMUD, the Modesto and Turlock irrigation districts, Roseville, Palo Alto, Alameda, Silicon Valley Power, Redding and Lodi to PG&E. It sends customers of Imperial Irrigation District, Riverside, Anaheim, Pasadena, Glendale, Burbank, Azusa, Colton and Banning to SoCalGas. LADWP handles its own customers, and Valley Electric Association customers go to SCE.

The assignment decides which pot you draw from. PG&E's $99 million AB 209 share reserves $31 million for customers of publicly owned utilities, and SCE's $87.3 million reserves $1 million. Those reserved sub-budgets, labeled POU on the tracker, are the only equity money shown as open. A SMUD customer applying through PG&E draws on an open budget. A Riverside customer applying through SoCalGas joins a waitlist.

sections.heading: SCE customers: what Edison requires
sections.body:
SCE says its ratepayer-funded SGIP budgets are closed to new applicants and that its state-funded equity budget has been exhausted and is on a waitlist. The tracker agrees: SCE's non-POU equity budget, the one that serves Edison's own customers, shows a waitlist.

SCE adds conditions of its own. It says every new customer must be interconnected with Permission to Operate on the Solar Billing Plan before an SGIP incentive is paid. It requires an SGIP-approved rate and lists TOU-D-PRIME, TOU-D-5-8PM and TOU-EV-1, which is closed to new customers. It says most new projects must enroll in a qualified demand response program, although the handbook exempts low-income equity applicants from that rule. SCE points customers to vendors on its Battery Marketplace and takes program questions at SGIPGroup@sce.com.

sections.heading: PG&E, SDG&E, SoCalGas and LADWP customers
sections.body:
PG&E's SGIP page says the equity rebate can cover up to 100 percent of cost for customers who meet the income test or are enrolled in CARE, FERA or ESA. It also says the rebate is closed and that waitlist applications go through your contractor. On the tracker, PG&E's budget for its own customers is waitlisted while its city-utility sub-budget is open.

In SDG&E's territory the Center for Sustainable Energy administers SGIP. Its AB 209 budget shows a waitlist, as do the SoCalGas and LADWP budgets. None of the three had open equity money on September 23, 2026.

sections.heading: What a waitlist means for your quote
sections.body:
A waitlist position is not a reservation. Waitlisted projects move up only if reserved projects drop out or money is shifted. The handbook says that after June 30, 2028, administrators transfer unallocated AB 209 funds to administrators that still have waitlists. Nobody can promise when, or whether, your turn comes.

So price the battery as if the incentive never arrives. Ask for an itemized quote with the incentive on its own line, then the amount you would owe if it is approved, if it is paid late, and if it is denied. If the project only works with the incentive, keep your place in line and hold off on signing. Get the application reference number and check its status with the administrator yourself.

sections.heading: How an application is filed
sections.body:
Homeowners rarely file alone. The CPUC and the utilities point customers to an installer or developer, who prepares the application and requests the reservation. The handbook makes the host customer, the utility customer of record at the site, the holder of the reservation, and lets the host customer name or replace the applicant, system owner and developer at any time.

Ask the developer in writing which budget and administrator it is applying to, which documents it needs from you, and who will receive the payment. Keep copies of everything submitted. If a salesperson says you qualify, ask which of the handbook's eligibility paths they relied on and what document proves it.

sections.heading: Other California battery rebates to check
sections.body:
SGIP is not the only program. PG&E's Permanent Battery Storage Rebate pays $7,500 to first-time battery owners with five or more Wildfire Safety outages since January 1, 2024. PG&E showed 179 rebates left as of September 18, 2026, with a December 31, 2026 deadline. PG&E's Residential Storage Initiative installs a battery at no charge for some income-qualified or medically vulnerable customers on circuits with repeated EPSS outages, and PG&E says its 2026 supply is almost gone. SCE's Critical Care Backup Battery program provides a portable battery to eligible Medical Baseline customers in high fire risk areas.

The federal credit is out of the picture for a battery you buy now. The IRS says the residential clean energy credit is not allowed for expenditures made after December 31, 2025.

whenThisIsWrong: Do not wait on SGIP if you need backup power before the next fire season: a waitlisted incentive cannot be counted on in time. Pause as well if the purchase only works with an incentive that has not been reserved, if the provider cannot name the budget and administrator, or if the contract asks for payment before you know whether funding is set aside for your project.

faqs.question: What is SGIP in California?
faqs.answer: The Self-Generation Incentive Program pays incentives for batteries and other equipment on the customer's side of the meter. The CPUC oversees it and PG&E, SCE, SoCalGas, the Center for Sustainable Energy and LADWP administer it. For homes today it means the income-qualified equity budget; the general-market budget is closed.

faqs.question: Who qualifies for California SGIP?
faqs.answer: For the equity budget on a single-family home: income at or below 80 percent of area median income, or income verified through CARE, FERA, ESA, SASH or DAC-SASH. Any California residential customer can apply, including city-utility customers. Renters need the owner's written approval.

faqs.question: Is SGIP still available in 2026?
faqs.answer: Only in part. On September 23, 2026 the tracker showed equity money open for city-utility customers assigned to PG&E or SCE, and waitlists for everyone else. Ratepayer-funded budgets stopped taking applications on December 30, 2025.

faqs.question: How much is the SGIP battery rebate?
faqs.answer: The equity budget pays $1.10 per watt-hour of storage plus $3.10 per watt for new solar. The handbook's example of a 13.2 kWh battery and 5 kW of solar reaches $30,020. The general-market budget's last step paid $0.15 per watt-hour, and it is closed.

faqs.question: Does SCE offer a battery rebate?
faqs.answer: SCE administers SGIP in its territory. It says its ratepayer budgets are closed and its equity budget is waitlisted, and it requires Permission to Operate on the Solar Billing Plan and an SGIP-approved rate before it pays an incentive.

faqs.question: Can CRR approve an SGIP application?
faqs.answer: No. California Rate Relief is a private solar referral service. The optional inquiry below collects project information for a referral. Incentive applications go to the program administrator, usually through your installer.

bottomLine: SGIP still exists for homes, but only as an income-qualified budget that is mostly waitlisted. Confirm your eligibility path and your administrator, check the live tracker, and price the battery without the incentive before you sign.

metaTitle: Tesla Powerwall 3 Cost in California (2026): Installed Price
metaDescription: What a Powerwall 3 costs installed in California in 2026: LBNL price data, what Tesla's quote covers, SGIP status on Sept. 23 and the NEM 3.0 math.
h1: Tesla Powerwall 3 Cost in California (2026): Installed Price, Incentives and Sizing
intro:
A single Tesla Powerwall 3 is likely to cost somewhere around $10,000 to $13,500 installed in California before any panel upgrade, based on the only primary benchmark available: Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory found that battery storage added roughly $750 to $1,000 per kWh to the price of paired residential systems installed in 2023, and a Powerwall 3 holds 13.5 kWh. Tesla itself does not print a price. Its Powerwall order page asks for your installation address before it shows anything, which we confirmed on September 23, 2026, so your number comes from a quote, not a price list.

Two things changed the math this year. The federal Residential Clean Energy Credit (Section 25D) no longer applies to a system installed after December 31, 2025, and most Self-Generation Incentive Program (SGIP) budgets for home batteries are closed. What is left is the reason most Californians buy a battery now: under the CPUC's net billing tariff, stored midday solar is worth more when you use it in the evening than when you export it. This page covers the price, the specs that move it, sizing, SGIP, the tax picture and what a battery can earn.

sections.heading: What Tesla's quote shows, and what to ask it to separate
sections.body:
Tesla sells Powerwall 3 through its own design tool and through certified installers. The design tool does not display a price until you enter the address where the battery will go, because the scope of work depends on your electrical panel, the wall or garage where the unit mounts, and whether you are adding solar at the same time. That is also why a price you read in a forum post or a sales flyer is not a number to budget around.

When the quote arrives, ask for it broken into lines. You want the battery hardware, any Expansion unit, the backup switching equipment, electrical labor, any main-panel upgrade or backup-loads subpanel, trenching or long conduit runs, permit and inspection fees, and any roof or stucco repair. A lump-sum figure hides the part of the job that varies most from house to house, which is the electrical work, and it makes a second quote impossible to compare line for line.

sections.heading: The installed-cost benchmark, and how to read your quote against it
sections.body:
Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory's Tracking the Sun report (2024 Edition) is the most careful public study of what homeowners actually paid. Its regression analysis implies a price premium of roughly $750 to $1,000 per kWh of storage for paired residential systems installed in 2023. For one 13.5 kWh Powerwall 3, that is about $10,100 to $13,500. It is a national estimate from 2023 installs, not a California quote, so treat it as a sanity check rather than a target.

LBNL's August 2026 data update adds two useful facts. Among residential systems bought with cash in 2025, the median price of a solar-plus-storage system was $2.1 per watt higher than a solar-only system. And about 80% of the installed-price data for paired systems came from California, so the benchmark is mostly built from California jobs.

To use it, take the battery-related lines of your quote, leave out any panel upgrade, and divide by the usable kWh you are buying. A result far above $1,000 per kWh is worth a question. The answer may be a legitimate one, such as a service upgrade your utility requires, but you should hear it before you sign.

sections.heading: Powerwall 3 specs that move the price
sections.body:
Tesla's 2025 datasheet lists 13.5 kWh of usable energy and on-grid output that can be configured at 5.8, 7.6, 10 or 11.5 kW. The unit has a built-in solar inverter with six maximum power point trackers and up to 20 kW of solar input. On a new solar-plus-battery job, that can remove the separate string inverter from the equipment list, which is part of why a combined Powerwall 3 job can cost less than the battery and inverter bought separately.

Tesla rates solar-to-home efficiency at 97.5% and solar-to-battery-to-home at 89%. The datasheet lists a 185 locked-rotor-amp load start rating, which matters if you want the battery to start a well pump or an air-conditioning compressor during an outage. The warranty is 10 years.

A site can hold up to four Powerwall 3 units and up to three Expansion units, seven units in total. At 13.5 kWh each, that is 94.5 kWh at the upper limit. Most homes buy one. LBNL reports that the median residential battery installed in 2025 was 13.5 kWh, the size of a single Powerwall.

sections.heading: How many Powerwalls do you need?
sections.body:
Start from the job you want the battery to do. If the goal is lower bills under net billing, size the battery to the evening use you want to cover, which you can read off 12 months of hourly or 15-minute interval data in your utility account. A household that uses 10 to 12 kWh between late afternoon and bedtime is already close to what one Powerwall 3 stores.

If the goal is backup, list the circuits you need during an outage: refrigerator, internet, lights, a well pump, medical equipment, perhaps one air-conditioning zone. Power, not energy, is usually the limit. One unit can deliver up to 11.5 kW continuously on grid, and heavy motor loads need the start rating noted above.

A second unit adds cost almost in proportion to the hardware, while the permit, the backup switching equipment and part of the electrical labor are paid once. Ask your installer to price one and two units on the same visit so you can see the real cost of the second 13.5 kWh.

sections.heading: Powerwall 3 under NEM 3.0 net billing
sections.body:
Customers of PG&E, SCE and SDG&E who applied to interconnect on or after April 15, 2023 take service on the CPUC's net billing tariff. The CPUC says the credit for exported solar is usually lower than the retail rate, though it can rise above it on late summer evenings, and that customers can maximize bill savings by pairing a battery so they use or export stored energy during those high-value hours. Nearly 70% of net-billing customers had paired a battery with solar by the end of 2024, according to the CPUC.

The spread you capture depends on your rate. The CPUC Public Advocates Office reported average residential rates of 33.7 cents per kWh at PG&E, 34.4 cents at SCE and 45.5 cents at SDG&E as of June 2026. Net-billing customers must take the rate the CPUC approved for them: E-ELEC at PG&E, TOU-D-PRIME at SCE and EV-TOU-5 at SDG&E. The original customer keeps the tariff for nine years, and residential PG&E and SCE customers who apply before the end of 2027 get slightly higher export credits for those nine years.

None of this applies to municipal utilities such as LADWP or SMUD, which set their own rates and export rules. If you are served by one, build the battery case from its tariff, not from NEM 3.0.

sections.heading: SGIP rebates in September 2026
sections.body:
The Self-Generation Incentive Program tracker, with data as of September 23, 2026, shows the general residential category, Small Residential Storage, closed at Step 7 in the PG&E, SCE, SoCalGas and CSE budgets. The ratepayer-funded Residential Solar and Storage Equity category, Equity Resiliency, and the San Joaquin Valley residential category also show closed.

The remaining door is Residential Solar and Storage Equity under AB 209, which pays $1.10 per Wh for storage at Step 6 and is limited by income and other eligibility rules. The tracker shows its budgets waitlisted for CSE, SoCalGas and LADWP, waitlisted in the PG&E and SCE non-POU budgets, and open in the PG&E and SCE POU budgets. A column on a tracker is not an eligibility decision, and a waitlist is not a promise of money. Confirm with the program administrator before you count on it.

sections.heading: Federal tax credits: buying versus leasing
sections.body:
If you buy the battery, with cash or a loan, there is no federal credit on a 2026 installation. IRS guidance on Public Law 119-21 says the Section 25D credit is not allowed for expenditures made after December 31, 2025, and that an expenditure counts as made when the original installation is completed. A deposit paid in 2025 does not carry the credit into a 2026 install.

Under a lease or power purchase agreement, the company that owns the equipment may claim the commercial credit under Section 48E. The statute ends that credit for solar and wind property placed in service after December 31, 2027 unless construction began in time, but it states that the cut-off does not apply to energy storage. Whether any of the owner's credit reaches you depends on the contract, so compare the monthly payment and escalator against a cash quote rather than assuming a lease passes the credit through.

sections.heading: What a Powerwall can earn in a virtual power plant
sections.body:
A battery can also be paid for helping the grid. Sunrun reported that on September 9, 2026, it and Tesla dispatched 580 MW from more than 140,000 home batteries across the PG&E, SCE and SDG&E service areas, including about 110,000 Tesla Powerwalls, under the California Energy Commission's Demand Side Grid Support program and the CPUC's Emergency Load Reduction Program.

DSGS runs from May to October and pays for committed capacity and for measured load reduction during extreme events. The CPUC says the residential part of ELRP, Power Saver Rewards, sunset at the end of the 2025 program year. Payment terms depend on the program and the company enrolling you, so ask for them in writing, including how much charge the battery keeps in reserve for your own outages.

sections.heading: Installer bankruptcies and your battery warranty
sections.body:
The 10-year Powerwall warranty comes from Tesla. The workmanship warranty, the roof-penetration warranty and any lease or PPA come from whoever sold and installed the system, and several of those companies have filed for bankruptcy. Federal court dockets show Freedom Forever LLC filed Chapter 11 in Delaware on April 15, 2026 (No. 26-10522), and the court signed an order converting the case to Chapter 7 on August 7, 2026. Sunnova Energy International filed Chapter 11 in the Southern District of Texas on June 8, 2025 (No. 25-90160). SunPower Corporation filed Chapter 11 in Delaware on August 5, 2024 (No. 24-11649).

Before you sign, ask who holds the workmanship warranty, who holds the agreement if it is a lease or PPA, and whether either can be sold or assigned. Check the contractor's license yourself at the Contractors State License Board.

sections.heading: Is Powerwall 3 worth it? A short review of the trade-offs
sections.body:
On paper, Powerwall 3's strengths are the integrated solar inverter, the 11.5 kW continuous output and the motor-start rating, which together let one unit run more of a house than older AC-coupled batteries could. The weaker points are the ones a spec sheet cannot fix: a 10-year warranty on equipment you may want to run longer than that, a price you only learn from a site-specific quote, and savings that depend on your rate plan and your evening use.

It tends to make sense when you are adding solar and a battery together on a net-billing rate, when outages are a real problem where you live, or when you can enroll in a paid grid program. It makes less sense when your evening use is small, when you are on a municipal utility with generous export terms, or when a working battery would be replaced mainly for the efficiency gain.

whenThisIsWrong: Slow down before buying a Powerwall 3 if any of these fit you. Your utility is municipal, such as LADWP or SMUD, so NEM 3.0 export credits and the IOU rate figures on this page do not apply and the case has to be rebuilt from your own tariff. Your evening use is small enough that most of a 13.5 kWh battery would sit unused on a normal day. You were counting on SGIP and have not confirmed with the program administrator that your household qualifies under AB 209 and that funds are available, not just waitlisted. You are replacing a working Powerwall 2 mainly for the efficiency gain. Or you are being pressed to sign a lease or PPA this week because a federal deadline is supposedly about to hit; the statute exempts storage from the 2027 solar and wind cut-off, so that pressure is a sales tactic.

faqs.question: How much does a Tesla Powerwall 3 cost installed in California?
faqs.answer: Tesla does not publish a price; its order page asks for your address first. The closest primary benchmark is LBNL's estimate that storage added roughly $750 to $1,000 per kWh to paired residential systems installed in 2023, which is about $10,100 to $13,500 for one 13.5 kWh Powerwall 3. A panel upgrade, a backup-loads subpanel or a long conduit run adds to that. Get an itemized quote and compare it line by line.

faqs.question: How much is a Powerwall without installation?
faqs.answer: Tesla does not sell Powerwall 3 as a hardware-only retail product with a published price, and its design tool quotes installed systems by address. Treat any hardware-only figure you see online as unverified, and ask the installer to show the hardware line separately in the quote.

faqs.question: Is there a program that pays for most or all of a Powerwall?
faqs.answer: Not for most households in 2026. The SGIP equity categories that used to cover much of a battery's cost pay $1.10 per Wh, about $14,850 for 13.5 kWh, but they are limited by income and other rules. As of September 23, 2026 the AB 209 equity budgets were waitlisted for CSE, SoCalGas and LADWP and in the PG&E and SCE non-POU budgets, and open in the PG&E and SCE POU budgets. Confirm eligibility with the administrator. Be wary of any offer that calls a battery costless; read who owns it and what you pay over the term.

faqs.question: Does Powerwall 3 qualify for the federal tax credit in 2026?
faqs.answer: Not if you own it. The IRS says Section 25D is not allowed for expenditures made after December 31, 2025, and an expenditure is made when installation is completed. Under a lease or PPA the owner may claim Section 48E, and whether that lowers your payment depends on the contract.

faqs.question: How many Powerwall 3 units can one home have?
faqs.answer: Tesla's datasheet allows up to four Powerwall 3 units and up to three Expansion units at one site, seven units in total, or 94.5 kWh at 13.5 kWh each. Most homes install one; LBNL reports the median residential battery installed in 2025 was 13.5 kWh.

faqs.question: Is Powerwall 3 worth it under NEM 3.0?
faqs.answer: It can be, because the CPUC says export credits under net billing are usually below the retail rate, so solar you store and use in the evening is worth more than solar you export. How much more depends on your rate plan and how much you use after sunset. Run 12 months of your own interval data before you decide.

faqs.question: Can a Powerwall earn money by sharing power with the grid?
faqs.answer: Yes, through programs such as the California Energy Commission's Demand Side Grid Support, which runs May to October and pays for capacity and load reduction during extreme events. Sunrun reported a September 9, 2026 dispatch of 580 MW from more than 140,000 home batteries under DSGS and ELRP. Terms vary by program and by the company that enrolls you.

bottomLine: Budget roughly $10,000 to $13,500 for one installed Powerwall 3 before any panel upgrade, based on LBNL's $750 to $1,000 per kWh storage premium, and expect the real number to come only from an address-specific quote. The federal 25D credit is gone for systems installed after 2025, and SGIP is closed for most households outside the income-limited AB 209 budgets. The case for the battery in 2026 rests on net billing: stored solar used in the evening is worth more than solar exported at midday, plus backup during outages and, in some cases, payments from grid programs. Get two itemized quotes, confirm your rate plan, and check who stands behind the workmanship warranty.

metaTitle: Tesla Powerwall Alternatives for California Homes 2026
metaDescription: Tesla Powerwall 3 alternatives compared: Enphase, FranklinWH and SolarEdge capacity, output, warranty, coupling and what drives installed price in California.
h1: Tesla Powerwall Alternatives for California Homes
intro:
A Tesla Powerwall 3 holds 13.5 kWh of usable capacity and outputs roughly 11.04 kW continuous, per Tesla's own datasheet. It's still the default quote from most California installers, but it's no longer the only serious option, and in some cases it isn't the best fit. Freedom Forever converted from Chapter 11 to Chapter 7 liquidation on August 7, 2026, leaving its homeowners without an installer of record. SunPower filed Chapter 11 in August 2024, and its SunVault battery is no longer sold new. LG Electronics has told customers directly it's exiting the home battery business worldwide — though as this page covers below, that notice doesn't reach LG's separate RESU battery line, which is still sold new. None of that is a knock on Tesla specifically — it's a sign of how thin the field of stable manufacturers has gotten, at the moment NEM 3.0 export credits, which the CPUC says are usually below the retail rate, have made batteries more important for PG&E, SCE and SDG&E customers.

This page compares what you can actually buy today from an installer likely to still be in business in three years: Enphase IQ Battery 5P and 10C, FranklinWH aPower 2, and SolarEdge Home Battery. It also explains, plainly, why LG Electronics' Home 8 and SunPower's SunVault are off the table for new purchases, why LG's RESU line isn't, and why the two numbers everyone asks about first — the federal tax credit and the SGIP rebate — are less generous in September 2026 than they were a year ago.

sections.heading: Why Californians Are Looking Past the Powerwall
sections.body:
Powerwall 3 remains the default recommendation from most installers, but 2026 changed the math for every battery brand, Tesla included. The federal Section 25D residential clean energy credit — the 30% credit — does not apply to expenditures made after December 31, 2025 under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA). A homeowner-purchased battery installed from January 1, 2026 onward gets zero federal credit, regardless of manufacturer.

At the same time, NEM 3.0, the net billing tariff covering PG&E, SCE, and SDG&E customers, credits exported solar at hourly values the CPUC says are usually lower than the retail rate, instead of the retail-rate credit legacy NEM 2.0 customers get. April 15, 2026 was the final cutoff for Permission-to-Operate under NEM 2.0 — any system permitted after that date is on NEM 3.0 regardless of when the paperwork started. If you're a PG&E, SCE, or SDG&E customer, a battery is the main way to use your own solar in the evening instead of exporting it for less than the retail rate. That's why alternatives matter now more than they did two years ago: more households are buying a battery at the same moment several major suppliers went out of business.

One caveat worth stating plainly: if you're served by a publicly owned utility — LADWP, SMUD, MID, Anaheim, Roseville, Lodi, Imperial Irrigation District, or Turlock Irrigation District — none of this NEM 3.0 urgency applies to you. Those utilities set their own net metering terms and aren't regulated by the CPUC. Check your own utility's tariff before assuming NEM 3.0 export credits apply to you.

sections.heading: Enphase IQ Battery 5P and 10C: The Modular, Widely Available Option
sections.body:
The IQ Battery 5P holds 5.0 kWh of usable capacity per module and is built to stack — most California installs run two or three units to approach or exceed Powerwall-class capacity. Continuous output is 3.84 kW per module, with a 7.68 kW peak sustained for 3 seconds (6.14 kW at 10 seconds), per Enphase's spec sheet. It's AC-coupled, using six embedded grid-forming microinverters per unit, which makes it a straightforward retrofit onto an existing non-Enphase solar system.

Warranty runs 15 years, five years longer than Tesla's 10-year term. Enphase's marketing materials cite up to 6,000 cycles; datasheets vary on whether the actual warranty trigger is 6,000 cycles or a 4,000-cycle/70%-capacity threshold, so get the current North American datasheet from your installer before treating either figure as guaranteed.

For a closer match to Powerwall 3's single-unit capacity, the IQ Battery 10C holds 10 kWh usable at 7.08 kVA continuous (240V), also AC-coupled and also carrying a 15-year warranty — but with a 60% capacity floor at warranty end, ten points lower than Tesla's 70% floor. That's a real trade-off: more years of coverage, but the battery is allowed to fade further before Enphase considers it out of warranty.

Enphase doesn't publish a consumer price, so get an itemized installed quote and divide it by usable kWh to compare. Many California installers offer Enphase batteries, and former SunPower SunVault customers are being offered them as a replacement path; ask your installer.

sections.heading: FranklinWH aPower 2: The Largest Single Box
sections.body:
The aPower 2 holds 15 kWh usable at 100% depth of discharge — more usable capacity in one unit than Tesla's 13.5 kWh Powerwall 3, and three times a single Enphase 5P module. Continuous output is 10 kW (about 40A at 240V) with a 15 kW peak, ahead of every other product in this comparison at the single-unit level.

It's AC-coupled, attaching downstream of an existing solar inverter, which makes it a clean retrofit choice regardless of what brand of panels or inverter you already have. FranklinWH also sells a separate DC-coupled unit, the aPower S, with an integrated hybrid inverter — don't confuse the two if a quote just says "FranklinWH"; ask which model is being installed.

Warranty runs 15 years or 60 MWh of cumulative throughput, whichever comes first — a usage-based cap rather than a straight cycle count, worth having your installer translate into your household's expected annual throughput.

The catch is the required aGate controller, mandatory hardware that adds to the price; ask for it as its own line on the quote. In exchange you get the largest expansion ceiling in this comparison: up to 225 kWh across 15 units on one aGate controller, well beyond Powerwall 3's three-expansion-pack limit of 54 kWh.

FranklinWH is a newer entrant to the California market. We could not confirm a California-specific installer count the way we could for Enphase — treat dealer availability as thinner than Tesla's or Enphase's network until your installer proves otherwise.

sections.heading: SolarEdge Home Battery: Only Right If You're Already on SolarEdge
sections.body:
The SolarEdge Home Battery (400V) holds 9.7 kWh usable at 100% depth of discharge, with 5 kW continuous output and a 7.5 kW peak for 10-second surges. Warranty is 10 years with a 70% capacity retention floor, matching Tesla's terms exactly.

The number that actually matters here is round-trip efficiency: SolarEdge cites approximately 94.5%, the highest of any product in this comparison. That's a direct result of DC coupling — the battery ties in before the inverter stage, so power skips the AC-to-DC-to-AC round trip an AC-coupled battery (Enphase, FranklinWH, or a retrofit Powerwall) requires. Fewer conversions means less energy lost as heat.

Here's the plain disqualifier: DC coupling means the SolarEdge Home Battery requires a SolarEdge Home Wave or StorEdge HD-Wave inverter. If your existing solar system isn't already built on SolarEdge equipment, this option mostly doesn't apply to you — swapping inverter brands just to add a battery rarely pencils out. This is a same-ecosystem product, not a universal retrofit battery, and any installer who doesn't say that upfront isn't being straight with you.

Scalability tops out at three units per inverter (about 29 kWh) or 87.3 kWh system-wide. SolarEdge doesn't publish a consumer installed price; get an itemized quote.

sections.heading: LG: One Battery Line Is Exiting, the Other Isn't
sections.body:
LG Electronics posted a notice on its own site stating it is "transitioning away from the energy storage business globally," while committing to continue honoring the limited warranty on units already installed. No wind-down date is given. Read the notice's own language carefully, though: it names LG Electronics ESS specifically and doesn't mention LG Energy Solution or LG Chem.

That distinction matters because two different LG entities sell into this space. LG Electronics made the complete Home 8 ESS unit, which resellers show discontinued as of December 2024 — that's the line the exit notice covers. LG Energy Solution (spun off from LG Chem in 2022) makes the separate RESU line of battery cells, and it is not exiting. The RESU Prime line is still sold new through authorized dealers as of 2026; get its current datasheet from the dealer for capacity, output and warranty terms. Some individual distributors dropped their own RESU Prime stock in late 2024, which may be where the "LG is done" impression comes from, but that's a distributor's inventory decision, not a manufacturer exit.

The bottom line for a California homeowner shopping today: don't treat "LG" as one answer. LG Electronics' Home 8 is discontinued — expect warranty support only, no new units, expansions, or software features. LG Energy Solution's RESU line, sold under a different corporate parent, is a real purchase option through authorized dealers. If an installer quotes "LG," ask which entity actually makes the unit before assuming it's off the table.

sections.heading: SunPower SunVault: Discontinued, and Existing Owners Should Know the Support Picture
sections.body:
SunPower Corp filed Chapter 11 in August 2024. Complete Solar, now Complete Solaria, bought the SunPower brand, trademarks, and dealer network in a sale that closed September 30, 2024 — but that sale explicitly did not transfer liability for systems, batteries, leases, or PPAs installed before that date. SunVault is not a product you can buy new today.

If you already own a SunVault battery, warranty and support are nominally routed through the Complete Solaria-operated successor channel and the mySunPower app. Multiple consumer-facing sources describe difficulty getting warranty traction and inconsistent software support — those specific complaints come from owner blogs and forums, not a court filing or company statement, so treat them as reported experience rather than confirmed policy. What is confirmed is the structural fact: the company that built your battery no longer exists in its original form, and the entity servicing it did not originally sell it to you.

For a reader asking whether they can still get a SunVault, the honest answer is no. For current SunPower-brand quotes, Complete Solaria-affiliated dealers are now installing Enphase batteries — specifically the IQ Battery 5P and 10C covered above — under the SunPower name, not a SunVault-branded product. If a "SunPower" quote in 2026 includes a battery, ask which manufacturer actually made it.

sections.heading: SGIP: Don't Count On It Before You Check
sections.body:
California's Self-Generation Incentive Program is the rebate every battery seller mentions and almost none describe accurately. As of September 22, 2026, the program's tracker at selfgenca.com/home/program_metrics shows the general-market Small Residential Storage category closed at Step 7 ($0.15 per Wh) for CSE, SCE, SoCalGas and PG&E customers.

The AB 209 Residential Solar and Storage Equity category ($1.10 per Wh) shows a waitlist for CSE, SoCalGas and LADWP customers, and the ratepayer-funded Residential Solar and Storage Equity category shows closed. Treat that as a snapshot, not a standing fact, and pull the tracker yourself the day you're ready to apply, for your own utility. A waitlist does not promise a rebate.

The Equity Resiliency category, the track aimed at medically vulnerable and wildfire-risk households, is also closed ($1.00 per Wh, Step 5).

sections.heading: The Federal Credit Is Gone for Purchases, Except Through a PPA
sections.body:
Section 25D, the 30% residential clean energy credit that used to apply to a homeowner-purchased battery, does not apply to expenditures made after December 31, 2025, under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. If you buy or finance a battery outright and it's installed in 2026 or later, there's no federal tax credit attached to it. That applies to every product in this comparison — Enphase, FranklinWH, SolarEdge, and Tesla alike.

There's one structural exception worth understanding, though not as a hard promise: third-party-owned systems (a lease or power purchase agreement, where a company owns the equipment and you pay for the output) can still access the commercial Section 48E investment tax credit, because the credit is claimed by the system's owner, not the homeowner. OBBBA tightened the 48E deadlines specifically for solar and wind generation — construction has to start by July 4, 2026, or the system has to be placed in service by December 31, 2027. Standalone battery storage was explicitly carved out of that tightened solar/wind timeline and appears to keep something closer to its original multi-year runway under 48E.

We're stating that directionally, not as an exact date. Several tax-policy sources converge on storage's ITC continuing on a longer schedule than solar or wind, but we did not pull IRS or Treasury primary text confirming a specific sunset year, so don't take a specific expiration year as fact from this page or from any installer's pitch. If a PPA structure is on the table for your battery, ask the provider to show you the underlying credit mechanics in writing rather than accepting a verbal promise about getting it before it expires.

Skip it if an installer's pitch leans on an SGIP rebate as a given — as of September 2026 the general-market track is closed, and quoting it as available is a red flag on the installer, not a reason to move faster. Treat a SunVault quote as a red flag outright — it isn't a real product to buy in 2026, whatever a dealer calls it. An LG quote needs one more question before you walk away from it: LG Electronics' Home 8 is gone, but LG Energy Solution's RESU line is still sold new through authorized dealers, so "LG" alone doesn't tell you which company you'd actually be buying from.

faqs.question: Is the Tesla Powerwall 3 still a good option in California?
faqs.answer: Yes, on the specs — 13.5 kWh usable, about 11.04 kW continuous output, a 10-year warranty with a 70% capacity floor, and Tesla's own installer network. It just isn't automatically the right answer anymore. FranklinWH beats it on single-unit capacity and output. Enphase beats it on warranty length and installer availability. Whether Powerwall 3 is your best fit depends on whether you want an integrated Tesla ecosystem or are retrofitting onto existing non-Tesla solar, where AC-coupled options like Enphase or FranklinWH may fit more cleanly.

faqs.question: Which battery has the most usable capacity in a single unit?
faqs.answer: FranklinWH's aPower 2, at 15 kWh usable and 100% depth of discharge — ahead of Tesla Powerwall 3's 13.5 kWh and SolarEdge's 9.7 kWh. Enphase's IQ Battery 5P is only 5 kWh per module, but it's built to stack, so a two- or three-unit Enphase system can match or exceed any single-unit competitor; you're trading single-box simplicity for modular scalability.

faqs.question: Can I still buy a SunPower SunVault or LG battery in 2026?
faqs.answer: SunVault, no — not sold new. SunPower Corp filed Chapter 11 in August 2024, and while Complete Solaria bought the SunPower brand and dealer network in September 2024, SunVault isn't a current product; SunPower-brand quotes now install Enphase batteries instead. LG is more nuanced: LG Electronics has exited the business and its Home 8 ESS is warranty-only, but LG Energy Solution — a separate company — still sells its RESU line, including the RESU16H Prime, through authorized dealers. If a quote includes "LG," ask specifically which LG entity and model it is before assuming it's unavailable.

faqs.question: Do I still get a federal tax credit for a home battery?
faqs.answer: Not if you buy or finance it outright. Section 25D, the residential clean energy credit, ended December 31, 2025 under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act — any battery purchased and installed in 2026 gets no federal credit, regardless of brand. The one exception is a third-party-owned lease or PPA, where the provider (not you) can potentially claim the commercial Section 48E credit, which storage kept on a longer runway than solar or wind under the same law. Ask any PPA provider to document the mechanics rather than taking a verbal promise.

faqs.question: Is SGIP still giving rebates for home batteries?
faqs.answer: Mostly no, as of September 22, 2026. The general-market Small Residential Storage category is closed at Step 7, and the Equity Resiliency category is closed too. The AB 209 Residential Solar and Storage Equity category shows a waitlist for CSE, SoCalGas and LADWP customers. Check selfgenca.com/home/program_metrics yourself, on the day you're ready to sign, before letting an installer's rebate math influence your decision.

faqs.question: What's the difference between AC-coupled and DC-coupled batteries, and does it matter?
faqs.answer: An AC-coupled battery (Enphase, FranklinWH, or a typical Powerwall retrofit) sits downstream of your existing solar inverter and works with almost any existing solar system — simpler retrofit, slightly more energy lost in conversion. A DC-coupled battery (SolarEdge Home Battery, or a high-voltage unit like LG's RESU16H Prime paired with a compatible hybrid inverter) ties in before the inverter stage, which raises round-trip efficiency but locks you into that inverter brand's ecosystem — it's a real option only if your existing equipment is already compatible.

faqs.question: Do I need a battery if I'm not on PG&E, SCE, or SDG&E?
faqs.answer: Probably not with the same urgency. NEM 3.0 and its export credits, which the CPUC says are usually below the retail rate, apply to CPUC-regulated investor-owned utilities: PG&E, SCE, and SDG&E. Publicly owned utilities — LADWP, SMUD, MID, Anaheim, Roseville, Lodi, Imperial Irrigation District, and Turlock Irrigation District — set their own net metering terms and aren't subject to NEM 3.0 at all. If you're served by one of these, check your own utility's export rate before assuming the battery math on this page applies to you.

bottomLine: If you're on PG&E, SCE, or SDG&E, a home battery matters more now that the CPUC says NEM 3.0 export credits are usually below the retail rate. Powerwall 3 (13.5 kWh, 11.04 kW continuous, 10-year warranty) is still a fine choice, but it isn't the only one. FranklinWH aPower 2 beats it on single-unit capacity (15 kWh) and output (10 kW continuous, 15 kW peak). Enphase IQ Battery 5P/10C carries a 15-year warranty and is widely offered by California installers. SolarEdge Home Battery only makes sense if you're already on SolarEdge inverters. SunPower SunVault is no longer sold new and is legacy-support-only. LG is split: LG Electronics has exited the business (warranty-only on Home 8), but LG Energy Solution's RESU line is still sold new through authorized dealers — don't treat "LG" as one answer. Don't let an installer's SGIP math or a vague "get it before the credit expires" line do the deciding for you: verify the SGIP status at selfgenca.com and ask a PPA provider to show the 48E mechanics in writing before you sign anything.

metaTitle: PG&E Permanent Battery Storage Rebate: $7,500 Rules
metaDescription: PG&E pays $7,500 toward a permanent home battery if you've had 5+ Wildfire Safety outages since 2024. Who qualifies, the ELRP rule and the 2026 deadline.
h1: PG&E Permanent Battery Storage Rebate: Who Gets the $7,500
intro:
PG&E's Permanent Battery Storage Rebate pays $7,500 after you buy and install a qualifying home battery, but only if your account has had five or more Wildfire Safety outages since January 1, 2024. You also have to be a first-time battery customer, be on a time-of-use rate, and enroll the battery in PG&E's Emergency Load Reduction Program through your battery provider.

The money is limited. PG&E's rebate page showed 200 rebates remaining as of September 14, 2026, on a first-come, first-served basis. You must apply within 12 months of receiving Permission to Operate or by December 31, 2026, whichever comes first.

This page walks through every condition in PG&E's terms, what the outage test means, which batteries and contracts are excluded, how the grid-event enrollment works, and what to look at if you don't qualify.
